                                            Pivotal, cluster and interface measures for critical
                                                             planar percolation
                                                  Christophe Garban                 Gábor Pete            Oded Schramm




arXiv:1008.1378v5 [math.PR] 13 Feb 2014
                                                                                    Abstract
                                                   This work is the first in a series of papers devoted to the construction and study
                                               of scaling limits of dynamical and near-critical planar percolation and related
                                               objects like invasion percolation and the Minimal Spanning Tree. We show here
                                               that the counting measure on the set of pivotal points of critical site percolation
                                               on the triangular grid, normalized appropriately, has a scaling limit, which is a
                                               function of the scaling limit of the percolation configuration. We also show that
                                               this limit measure is conformally covariant, with exponent 3/4. Similar results
                                               hold for the counting measure on macroscopic open clusters (the area measure),
                                               and for the counting measure on interfaces (length measure).
                                                   Since the aforementioned processes are very much governed by pivotal sites,
                                               the construction and properties of the “local time”-like pivotal measure are key
                                               results in this project. Another application is that the existence of the limit
                                               length measure on the interface is a key step towards constructing the so-called
                                               natural time-parametrization of the SLE6 curve.
                                                   The proofs make extensive use of coupling arguments, based on the separa-
                                               tion of interfaces phenomenon. This is a very useful tool in planar statistical
                                               physics, on which we included a self-contained Appendix. Simple corollaries of
                                               our methods include ratio limit theorems for arm probabilities and the rotational
                                               invariance of the two-point function.

1    Introduction
Critical planar percolation has become a central object of probability theory and sta-
tistical mechanics; see [Gri99, Wer07] for background. A main reason for this is that
the discrete process is known to have an interesting continuum scaling limit, in several
different but closely related senses, and this scaling limit has turned out to be very
useful in understanding also the discrete process, even more than Brownian motion
helps in understanding random walks. However, in passing to any notion of a scaling
limit, some microscopic information is always lost, and it is far from clear what natural
discrete objects (functions of the discrete percolation configuration) will have limits
that are meaningful in the scaling limit. This paper focuses on the scaling limits of
counting measures on different types of special points of the discrete percolation con-
figuration, normalized by a quantity comparable to their expected value, so that they
have a chance to produce a finite limit. The main types of special points that one might
think of are the following:
1) macroscopic open clusters: points that are contained in open clusters that have
a macroscopic size (clusters that are still visible in the scaling limit);
2) interfaces: points on interfaces separating macroscopic open and closed clusters, or
the points on a single exploration path that converges to SLE6 ;
3) exterior boundaries of clusters: points on interfaces that are not separated from
infinity (or from the boundary of the domain) by the interface itself; for instance, the
lowest open left-right crossing in a rectangular domain;
4) pivotal points: a bit (vertex in site percolation or edge in bond percolation) is
called pivotal for some macroscopic crossing event in a given percolation configuration
if flipping its state (open versus closed) changes the outcome of the event.
    Having scaling limits for these normalized counting measures is analogous to the
construction of the local time measure of one-dimensional Brownian motion at zero via
the counting measure on the zeroes of random walks. However, the proofs here are
much harder, since we do not have the one-dimensional Markov structure that makes
the number of zeroes in two disjoint time intervals independent once we condition on
the value of the Brownian motion at any one moment between the two intervals.
    The reason for our paper is the applications of these limit measures. The quantity
of pivotal points governs several fundamental dynamical processes related to critical
percolation: dynamical percolation, the near-critical ensemble (percolation in
the critical window), and related near-critical objects like invasion and gradient per-
colation and the Minimal Spanning Tree. Our present work is the first paper in a
series devoted to the construction and study of the scaling limits of these processes.
    Why are these processes so fundamental? The scaling limit of dynamical percolation
is going to be the natural time evolution with stationary measure being the conformally
invariant continuum percolation. The near-critical regime is of central interest in re-


                                           3
lation with any critical system; e.g., as critical planar systems are often described by
conformal (massless) field theories in physics, their near-critical versions are described
by massive field theories. Invasion percolation is a self-organized criticality version of
percolation. Finally, the Minimal Spanning Tree, besides being a classical combina-
torial object, is a natural candidate to possess a scaling limit that is invariant under
translations, rotations and scaling, but not under general conformal maps.
    Now, how is the scaling limit of the pivotal measure a key to the understanding of the
scaling limits of these processes? Any description of continuum critical percolation is
intimately related to macroscopic crossing events. Hence, in any reasonable dynamics,
the effect of the dynamics on the pivotal points for macroscopic crossing events will
probably determine the macroscopic evolution of the system: if, in a given configuration,
there are more pivotals for a crossing event, then the dynamics will change that event
more easily. However, the amount of pivotals for a macroscopic crossing event is, a
priori, microscopic data, so it is not clear that the dynamics will make sense also in the
scaling limit. The results of the present paper say that we can in fact tell the number of
pivotals from macroscopic information only, and hence we can hope to build the scaling
limits of these processes from continuum percolation plus extra randomness governing
how pivotals are changing. Such a description also opens the way to understand the
conformal properties of the dynamics. These are the goals of this project.
    In another direction, the construction of these measures is closely related to the
question of finding a so-called natural (or physical) time-parametrization for SLE
curves related to percolation, as opposed to the usual parametrization using conformal
half-plane capacity.
    In this introduction, we will first discuss these applications in more detail (this time
with references), then explain the results of the present paper, together with the main
tools and ideas used in the proofs.

1.1    Applications to dynamical and near-critical percolation
Throughout the paper, we will restrict our attention to critical site percolation on the
triangular grid ηT with small mesh size η > 0, where each vertex of the grid is chosen
to be “open” or “closed” with probability 1/2, independently of each other. This is the
model where conformal invariance [Smi01] and its consequences are known: convergence
of the exploration interface to SLE6 [Sch00, Smi01, Smi06, CN07] and existence of a full
scaling limit as a collection of interface loops [CN06]. See [Wer07] for a nice textbook
account of the subject.
    Some partial results remain valid for Z2 , for subsequential scaling limits of percola-
tion, which we will discuss at the end of Subsection 1.3.
    In dynamical percolation at criticality, a model introduced by [HgPS97] and
Itai Benjamini, independently, each bit is changing its state back and forth between
open and closed using independent Poisson clocks, with rates in the two directions
that make the stationary measure of this process just critical percolation (i.e., for site

                                             4
percolation on ηT, where pc = 1/2, the two rates are equal). Two related questions
on this process have been studied: 1) How does noise affect the macroscopic features
of the system (e.g., how much time is needed for the event of having an open left-right
crossing in a large square to decorrelate)? 2) On the infinite lattice, are there random
exceptional times at which the configuration satisfies events that almost surely do not
happen in the stationary measure? See [Gar11, Ste09] for surveys of noise sensitivity
and dynamical percolation, respectively. For critical planar percolation, both questions
have been answered quite completely in a series of three papers over a decade [BKS99,
SSt10, GPS10a]: the time (the amount of noise) needed for decorrelation is given by
the typical number of pivotal points, in the following way.
    A “quad” Q is a simply connected planar domain with piecewise smooth boundary
and four marked points {a, b, c, d} ∈ ∂Q. We think of Q as given independently of
the grid ηT, with roughly unit size. Site percolation on ηT can be considered as a
two-coloring of the faces of the hexagonal lattice, and hence we can talk about an open
crossing in a percolation configuration ωη from the “left” boundary arc ab to the “right”
boundary arc cd using the hexagons intersecting Q. Since the probability of this left-
right crossing converges to a conformally invariant quantity crQ ∈ (0, 1) as η → 0, it
is very natural to focus on these macroscopic crossing events when considering scaling
limits. Now notice that a site x (i.e., a hexagon) is pivotal in a given configuration for
left-right crossing if and only if there are open arms from it to ab and cd and closed
arms to bc and da, i.e., if it satisfies the alternating four-arm event to ∂Q (with the
arms ending at the respective boundary pieces). For most points x ∈ Q (in the “bulk”),
the probability of this event is comparable (up to multiplicative factors depending on Q
and on what we mean by “bulk”) to α4η (η, 1), the alternating four-arm probability from
distance η to 1 on ηT. See Subsection 2.1 for more on notation and the basics. In fact, it
is not hard to show that the expected number of pivotal points in Q is Q η −2 α4η (η, 1),
which is known to be η −3/4+o(1) on ηT. (Note that it is going to infinity as η → 0.)
In dynamical percolation, the state of a quad (if it is crossed from left to right or not)
changes exactly when the clock of a current pivotal point rings. Therefore, if we take
the rate of the clocks in dynamical percolation to be
                       r(η) := η 2 α4η (η, 1)−1 (= η 3/4+o(1) on ηT) ,
then, after time t, by the linearity of expectation and Fubini, the expected number
of pivotal switches (i.e., the number of changes of the crossing event) will be of
order t, with factors depending, of course, on Q: for a larger quad there are more
pivotals, hence more changes, in expectation. This dynamical percolation process will
be denoted by {ωη (t)}t≥0 . The previous expectation result already tells us, by Markov’s
inequality, that in a short time interval [0, t], the probability of seeing any change is
small. However, for large t, the large expectation does not imply that there is a change
with high probability, so it is not immediately clear that this r(η) is really the right
scaling if we want to follow the changes in macroscopic crossing events.
    The possible issues are explained in [GPS10a], so we give only a brief summary.

                                             5
First of all, the expected number of pivotals for certain Boolean functions is much larger
than their typical number. E.g., for√the majority function on 2n + 1 bits, n + 1 bits are
pivotal with probability around 1/ n, but there are no pivotals with probability close
to 1. However, it is well-known that this issue does not happen with left-right crossing.
This is good, but even if we assumed more, namely, that for a large time t with high
probability there are many pivotal switches, it could be the case that pivotal switches
happen much faster in one direction than in the other, thus, at any given deterministic
moment, the quad is much more likely to be in one of the states (probably the starting
one). So, a priori, real macroscopic changes could start happening only at much larger
time scales than the one we chose by setting our r(η).
    The solution to these matters is to use discrete Fourier analysis instead of trying to
follow pivotals. With this tool, it is easy to show that at time t = 1 the correlation
                                                                                2
                   P Q is crossed in both ωη (0) and ωη (t) − P Q is crossed in ωη
     corrη (t) :=                                                     2
                            P Q is crossed in ωη − P Q is crossed in ωη
will already be bounded away from 1, hence a pivotal switch has happened with pos-
itive probability, and macroscopic changes have visibly started. (This result follows
from (1.2) of [GPS10a], using only the first and second moments of the size of the
so-called Fourier spectral sample of the crossing event, which happen to coincide with
the corresponding moments for the pivotal set.) It is much harder to prove, and this is
the main result of [GPS10a], that corrη (t) → 0 as t → ∞, uniformly in η. (This needs
precise estimates on the lower tail of the size of the spectral sample.) This was proved
even for bond percolation on ηZ2 , while, for the left-right crossing of the square [0, 1]2
in site percolation on ηT, also the rate corrη (t)  t−2/3 was established.
    Our present paper is independent of [GPS10a] and does not use Fourier analysis.
The above discussion is only to argue that r(η) = η 2 α4η (η, 1)−1 is the right scaling for
the scaling limit of dynamical percolation. However, we still have to explain what kind
of scaling limit we want to establish and how we will do this.
    As introduced in [SSm11] and discussed in Subsection 2.2 below, a percolation con-
figuration ωη on some domain Ω can be considered as a (random) point in a compact
metrizable space (HΩ , TΩ ) that encodes all macroscopic crossing events (the states of
all quads). The scaling limit ω of static percolation is the weak limit of the percolation
measures as η → 0, w.r.t. the topology of this compact space. The uniqueness of this
quad-crossing limit measure follows from [CN06], using the uniqueness of another notion
of scaling limit (based on interface loops), as we will explain in Subsection 2.3. We chose
to work in the quad-crossing space (HΩ , TΩ ) because following the states of a countable
dense family of quads in dynamical percolation is a very natural way of describing the
dynamics; for instance, the correlation decay results of [GPS10a] are formulated for
crossing events. Also, this way, {ωη (t)}t≥0 is a continuous time Markov process in the
compact space (HΩ , TΩ ), which certainly makes tightness arguments easier. One can
easily describe a natural space-time topology in which the processes {ωη (t)}t≥0 should
converge to some {ω(t)}t≥0 .

                                            6
    How can we try to describe this scaling limit? For a fixed η > 0, knowing the
number of pivotal sites for each quad in the plane at any given moment means that we
know the rates at which pivotal switches occur, hence we know the rate of transitions
for our Markov process. However, in the scaling limit there are no pivotal sites anymore
that we could count. So, an obvious first task is to show that the scaling limit µQ of the
normalized counting measure on the pivotals for a quad Q in ωη exists and is a function
of the static scaling limit ω. This is the main subject of the present paper. Then, one
can hope to build the scaling limit of dynamical percolation from the starting static
scaling limit configuration ω(0) plus independent Poisson clocks with rates given by µQ
for each Q: in the dynamics, when a pivotal switch of a quad happens, we change all
the crossing events appropriately, read off the new pivotal measure for each quad, and
continue. This was the suggestion of [CFN06], and it has the virtue that it is built
from critical percolation (plus some extra randomness), whose conformal properties
can be used to understand the dynamics, as well. Of course, there are some issues
here to deal with. For the many small quads inside a bounded domain there are many
pivotal sites, hence pivotals for small quads are switching almost all of the time, so
there is no nice ordering of all the pivotal switches. One can try to introduce a cut-off
 > 0, consider only quads of size larger than , then show that the dynamical picture
stabilizes as  → 0. A related question is whether ω(t), the states of all the macroscopic
quads at any time t > 0, is determined by the starting macroscopic configuration and
the macroscopic pivotal switches in [0, t], or rather there is a cascade of information
during the dynamics from the microscopic to the macroscopic world, i.e., microscopic
information we have forgotten in the scaling limit becomes macroscopically relevant at
later times. Such a cascade would certainly exclude the existence of the macroscopic
process {ω(t)}t≥0 as a Markov process. These stability results and the existence and
Markovianity of the dynamical percolation scaling limit are established in the sequel
paper [GPS13a]. In the present paper we also show how the conformal invariance
properties of critical percolation translate to conformal covariance properties of the
measures µQ , which will imply similar properties for the dynamical percolation scaling
limit.
    Dynamical percolation also provides us with tools to understand the near-critical
regime. Namely, if we modify the dynamics to always switching to “open” when a clock
rings, then, as time goes on, we are getting a more and more supercritical picture. As
times flows in the negative direction, we always turn sites to “closed”, getting a more and
more subcritical picture. All these pictures of different densities are naturally coupled
into one ensemble by the dynamics, where, as it is easy to check, the probability of a
site being open at time t ∈ (−∞, ∞) is 1/2 plus asymptotically to t r(η)/2 as η → 0.
(Still using the rates r(η) = η 2 α4η (η, 1)−1 → 0.) An equivalent but more standard
coupling of these configurations is done by assigning an independent Unif[0, 1] label to
every site, and defining the configuration ω̂η (λ) by declaring a site open if its label is
at most 1/2 + λ r(η). This {ω̂η (λ)}λ∈(−∞,∞) is called the near-critical ensemble, or


                                            7
percolation in the critical window. Why? From the dynamical percolation results
of [GPS10a] described above, it clearly follows that for large λ > 0 the probability
of having a left-right open crossing in a given quad Q is close to 1, while for λ < 0
very negative, the probability is close to 0, uniformly in η. A priori, this transition
could happen even faster, in a smaller window around criticality than the dynamical
percolation scale r(η), since monotonicity helps us. Nevertheless, it was shown already
by Kesten [Kes87] that the four-arm probabilities stay comparable to the critical α4η (η, 1)
in the entire regime 1/2+λ r(η), λ ∈ (−∞, ∞) (with the factors of comparability getting
worse as |λ| → ∞), and this implies (using Russo’s formula and differential inequalities)
that the probability of an open crossing cannot change so fast with λ that it reaches
0 or 1 before λ = ±∞. That it does reach 0 and 1 at the endpoints λ = ±∞ of this
r(η)-window was shown in [BCKS01]. This is simpler than establishing the dynamical
percolation window, and does not need Fourier analysis, somehow because this can now
be understood as a question about a single configuration ω̂η (λ) instead of a long time
interval. Also, the previously mentioned stability result for dynamical percolation that
we prove in [GPS13a] can be considered as a generalization of Kesten’s stability result
for the four-arm probabilities.
    In [GPS13a], in a way very similar to dynamical percolation, and still roughly fol-
lowing the suggestions of [CFN06], we prove that the η → 0 limit of the near-critical
ensemble {ω̂η (λ)}λ∈(−∞,∞) exists and is a Markov process in λ. This refines [BCKS01]
by showing the convergence of the crossing probabilities, and suggests convergence of
the distributions of the sizes of largest components for any fixed λ ∈ (−∞, ∞). It also
refines [NW09] by showing that the near-critical interface does have an actual scaling
limit (the so-called massive SLE6 ), not just subsequential limits. Massive SLEκ curves
are discussed in [MS10], but progress is reported only for certain special values of κ:
2, 4, 8, and some partial results for 16/3 and 3. It is also explained there why these
SLE-related curves are “massive”. We hope that our techniques will give a differential
equation for the Loewner driving function of the √ massive SLE6 , at least on the conjec-
tural level. This has the usual Brownian term 6Bt , plus a self-interacting drift term.
One drawback is that we do not see how this equation could lead to exact computations
like deducing Cardy’s crossing formula in the ordinary case.
    The near-critical ensemble is also closely related to other objects, like gradient
and invasion percolation and the Minimal Spanning Tree. The existence and
properties of the gradient percolation scaling limit are proved in [GPS13a], while for
the other two, in [GPS13b]. Since [GPS10b] already contains an informal description
of the main ideas, we will not discuss these models here.
    Finally, let us mention that a very different type of limit object for dynamical
percolation, the construction of a local time on the set of exceptional percolation times,
will appear in [HmPS12].




                                             8
1.2    The question of natural time-parametrization for SLE curves
The item labels 1)-4) in the very first paragraph of this Introduction correspond to
the number of macroscopic arms that a corresponding special point must have. So, it
should not be surprising if analogs of the above 4-arm results hold also for other k-arm
events. In the present subsection, we discuss the 2-arm case in a bit more detail, since
it is interesting also from a different point of view.
     SLE’s have been extremely useful in understanding discrete processes with confor-
mally invariant scaling limits. But there is also an opposite direction: if an SLE is
known to be the scaling limit of a discrete process, then we often gain valuable extra
information about the SLE. For instance, the reversibility of SLEκ for the special val-
ues κ = 2, 4, 6, 8 was known, using the discrete processes converging to them, much
before the general κ ≤ 4 result of Dapeng Zhan [Zha08]. The question of natural
time-parametrizations of SLE curves has to do with both directions.
     By definition, the standard time-parametrization for SLEκ is half-plane capacity
for the chordal and disk capacity (conformal radius) for the radial processes. These
parametrizations transform nicely under conformal maps, hence are often useful when
working with SLE’s — except, for instance, when one wants to consider the path tra-
versed in the reverse direction. On the other hand, the discrete processes converging to
SLE’s are naturally equipped with a time parametrization, given by the number of dis-
crete lattice steps, which obviously has nothing to do with the capacity parametrization
of the scaling limit. For instance, it has a locality property that capacity does not have,
namely, congruent pieces in two curves have the same length, regardless of the rest of
the curves. If the limit of the discrete time-parametrization existed, it should inherit
all these natural properties, and, in fact, it should be the d(κ)-dimensional Minkowski
content, where d(κ) = 1 + κ/8 is the dimension of the SLEκ [Bef08].
     After weaker results by [LS11], it was proved in [LZ13] that SLEκ for all κ < 8 has
a unique time-parametrization that satisfies a few natural conditions, such as the right
d(κ)-dimensional transformation rule (i.e., d(κ)-dimensional conformal covariance). An
improved proof, which also gives some information about regularity properties of the
parametrization, appeared recently in [LR12a]. Even more recently, it has been proved
in [LR12b] that this time-parametrization equals the d(κ)-dimensional Minkowski con-
tent. However, it is not known for a single κ that this parametrization is a limit of the
natural discrete parametrization of counting steps.
     In the present paper, the scaling limit of the normalized counting measure on a
percolation interface (see (1.3) below) will be handled quite similarly to the case of
pivotals, with two main differences: one, points on an interface between two boundary
points a, b ∈ ∂Q are characterized by having one open and one closed arm to the
respective boundary arcs ab and ba, instead of four alternating arms; two, it turns out
to be simpler and more natural to describe the scaling limit of the measure as a function
of the SLE6 interface, rather than a function of the entire percolation configuration in
the quad-crossing topology (see Subsection 5.3). Now, having constructed this scaling


                                            9
limit and having proved that it has the right conformal covariance properties, it looks
quite obvious that it is the natural time-parametrization we are looking for. However,
there is an issue: we have the length measure of the entire interface from a to b and
the measure restricted to small boxes, but any small box can contain several connected
pieces of the interface, and the measure of the box does not differentiate between the
pieces. So, it is not clear that we can also get the length measure of all the starting
segments of the interface. This question, together with fine metric properties (e.g.,
Hölder-regularity) of the length measure will be addressed in [GP].

1.3    The main results and techniques
Having been bombarded by two subsections of future applications, the reader hopefully
has a good idea by now what the results themselves are. Nevertheless, here they are
explicitly. For any missing definition, see Section 2.
   Let Ω ⊂ Ĉ = C ∪ {∞} be open, and (HΩ , TΩ ) be its quad-crossing space. For any
quad Q ⊆ Ω with piecewise smooth boundary, consider the following measure on Q, a
function of the discrete percolation configuration ωη ∈ HΩ :

is a complete, metrizable, separable space in the weak*-topology (also called the weak
convergence of measures).

                                                   10
    On a heuristic level, the scaling exponent 3/4 comes from the fact that µQ is a
“natural” measure supported on the set of pivotal points, which is known to be of
Hausdorff-dimension 3/4. (This dimension is not proved explicitly anywhere, but fol-
lows from a simple modification of [LSW01, Section 6.1] and the techniques of [Bef04].
See also [GPS10a, Theorem 10.4] for a very similar result. For more on the connections
between the dimension of a set and the measures supported, see [Mat95, Chapter 8].)
Of course, to make this explanation more grounded, one would also need to prove that
the support of the measure µQ (ω) is exactly the set of Q-pivotal points of ω, not just
a subset. This requires some work, which will be done in [GP].
    Note that it might be more natural to use a different family of measures: instead of
a measure for each quad Q ⊆ Ω, there could be a measure µ̄ρη for each radius ρ > 0, the
normalized counting measure on the ρ-important sites, i.e., sites x ∈ Ω that have the
alternating four-arm event from x to distance at least ρ. However, these ρ-important
measures are slightly cumbersome to deal with, so we will introduce one more family of
measures: the normalized counting measure µA   η on the so-called A-important sites,
where A ⊂ Ω is a topological annulus with piecewise smooth boundaries (called a proper
annulus). See Subsection 4.1 for the definitions, Theorems 4.3 and 6.1 for the results,
and Subsection 4.7 for a comparison between the ρ-important and A-important families
of measures.
    The case of the 1-arm event, i.e., the normalized counting measure on macroscopic
open clusters, is simpler than the case of pivotals, due to the monotonicity of the 1-
arm event that is false for the alternating 4-arm event. The actual formulation that we
will prove concerns the following measure (using the 1-arm analogue of the A-important
points mentioned above):
                                                X                   η2
                         λA    A
                          η = λη (ωη ) :=                   δx              ,           (1.2)
                                                                 α1η (η, 1)
                                            x∈∆: {x↔∂2 A}


where A is a proper annulus with outer boundary ∂2 A and inner disk ∆. See Subsec-
tions 5.1 and 6.4 for the results. Since α1η (η, 1) = η 5/48+o(1) , the covariance exponent is
91/48 in this case.
    Let us note that the cluster measure was also considered in [CN09] for percolation
and the FK-Ising model. In the case of FK percolation, as explained there, proving a
scaling limit result (similar to ours) for the area measure on FK clusters would enable
one to construct a magnetization field for the scaling limit of the Ising spin model.
In [CN09], Camia and Newman sketched the proof for the tightness of the normalized
discrete measures, while the main step in this program, i.e., the question of convergence,
is proved in [CGN12].
    The 2-arm case, i.e., the counting measure on the interfaces, will be slightly dif-
ferent. The setting is that Ω is a domain with smooth boundary and the so-called
Dobrushin boundary conditions: two marked points a, b ∈ ∂Ω, and we are interested in

                                              11
the set of edges of the triangular grid that have one endpoint connected to the boundary
arc ab by an open path, and another endpoint connected to the arc ba by a closed path,
in the configuration ωη . Of course, one usually considers dual edges, i.e., edges on the
hexagonal lattice that form the boundary of the open cluster of hexagons connected to
ab, thus forming an interface γη from a to b. The normalized counting measure is now
                                                                X                  η2
                 τηΩ,a,b = τηΩ,a,b (ωη ) = τηΩ,a,b (γη ) :=                δe              .   (1.3)
                                                              edges e∈γη
                                                                                α2η (η, 1)

    As mentioned in Subsection 1.2, it will be easier and more natural to show that the
limit measure τ Ω,a,b exists as a function of not the continuum percolation ω, an element
of the quad-crossing space HΩ , but as a function of the SLE6 limit of the interface γη .
See Subsection 5.3 for more details and the limit measure result, and Subsection 6.4 for
conformal covariance. The covariance exponent is 7/4.
   It would also be natural to consider the 3-arm case, i.e., points on the exterior
boundary of large clusters or of a single interface. However, this has some additional
technicalities that would make this paper even longer, while the results do not seem to
have striking applications at present, hence we chose not to address this case in detail.
See Subsection 5.4 for what the issues are and for hints on how they could be solved.
    Let us now explain the main ideas in the proofs of Theorems 1.1 and 1.2, together
with some lemmas that are interesting also in their own rights.
    First of all, as we said in Subsection 1.1, we want to prove the existence and con-
formal covariance of a measure that is measurable with respect to the Borel-σ-field of
the quad-crossing space (HΩ , TΩ ), see Subsection 2.2. Therefore, it is essential to
know that the discrete percolation configurations ωη themselves have a unique scaling
limit ω in this space. (As it will be apparent from the proof, if we had only subse-
quential limits of percolation, then we could not show the conformal covariance of the
subsequential limits of the measures.) However, [SSm11], where this space was intro-
duced, proves the existence and the “black noise factorization property” only along
subsequences. Fortunately, the uniqueness of the quad-crossing limit follows eas-
ily from the results of [CN06]: Camia and Newman showed there that the percolation
configuration described as the set of all interface loops has a unique and conformally
invariant scaling limit, and they also showed that the SLE6 interface in a subdomain
with Dobrushin boundary conditions can be extracted from their scaling limit. This
immediately implies that the quad-crossing events are also measurable in this scaling
limit. So, the quad-crossing scaling limit is a function of a unique scaling limit object,
hence is unique itself. This will be explained more in Subsection 2.3. From this we also
get that the quad-crossing scaling limit is conformally invariant, which would not follow
simply from Smirnov’s theorem of the conformal invariance for a single quad [Smi01]:
we need conformal invariance of the joint laws, not only the one-dimensional marginals
provided by the Cardy-Smirnov formula. After uniqueness, we need to know that, e.g.,

                                                 12
the four-arm event in an annulus is actually a measurable function of the quad-crossing
configuration ω and its probability is the η → 0 limit of the probabilities in the ωη
configurations. Though not obvious, this is not hard, and is done in Subsection 2.4.
All these measurability results are parts of the general belief that the different notions
of the full scaling limit for percolation are all equivalent. See [SSm11] for an overview
of these matters.
     Given the measurability results of the previous paragraph, one can start showing
that the number of Q-pivotals in any ball B ⊆ Q can be read off from macroscopic
quad-crossing events only, so that the values µQ   η (B) will have a chance to have a limit
that is a measurable function of ω. The main idea is to take a grid of macroscopic but
small mesh size , count the number Yη of -boxes in the grid that lie in B and have the
four-arm event to ∂Q, and hope that, for small , this number will give a good idea of
the number Xη of actual pivotal sites in B. To realize this hope, one needs to show that
given that an -box Qi has the four-arm event to ∂Q, the distribution of the pivotal
points inside Qi is more or less independent of the percolation configuration outside
an enlarged box kQi , with some large k. With enough independence, one could try to
prove a law of large numbers type result, saying that the contributions of the many
-boxes average out, so that Xη will be well-approximated (up to a factor 1 + o(1)) by
Yη times a deterministic factor β(η, ), which is basically the expectation of the number
of pivotals in an -box given that the box has the four-arm event to ∂Q. How do we fill
in the details? One way to express the approximate independence is that given that Qi
has the four-arm event to ∂Q, and given two different copies of the entire percolation
configuration outside kQi that satisfy the conditioning, the configurations inside Qi
can be coupled with large probability to agree in the two copies. Such coupling
results are proved in Section 3, using the separation of interfaces phenomenon
that is discussed in Appendix A. This coupling property is closely related (for the one-
arm event) to Kesten’s construction of the Incipient Infinite Cluster [Kes86], and (for
the multi-arm events, where the separation of interfaces starts playing a role) to the
construction of the multi-arm IIC measures by [DS11]. In fact, the proof strategy in our
Appendix A is based on [DS11]. Then, we use our coupling results in Section 4 to gain
enough independence to prove the approximation of Xη by β(η, )Yη in the L2 -sense.
Then there is some additional work in showing that the normalized counting measures
µQη (B) actually have a limit. The existence of this limit measure, and also its scale
invariance, use the following ratio limit theorems, proved in Subsection 4.5:
                              α4η (η, r)       α4 (, r)
                           lim η         = lim           = r−5/4 ,                    (1.4)
                          η→0 α4 (η, 1)    →0 α4 (, 1)

where α4 without the superscript η is the continuum four-arm probability, given by
SLE6 . See Remark 4.10 for an explanation why this is not at all obvious from the
four-arm exponent being 5/4. Similar limit results hold for the α1 and α2 probabilities,
                                                                            ωη 
and we prove the rotational invariance of the two-point function P x ←→ y in
the η → 0 limit, see Subsection 5.2.

                                            13
    For the proof of conformal covariance in Section 6, we have to deal with the fact
that a conformal map distorts the -grid that we use for the approximation, so we
need to compare such a distorted approximation with the original. Locally, each -box
alone is not much distorted, almost just shifted, rotated and scaled, so we can start
by proving the approximation results for all translated, rotated and scaled versions of
the -grid, which are still proper grids. However, if we tried to approximate locally the
distorted grid everywhere at the same time, by covering the domain by small pieces of
these proper grids, it would be impossible to glue these pieces so that we get a one-fold
covering of the domain, counting every pivotal exactly once. The solution is to take an
average of all the shifted and rotated approximations, w.r.t. the uniform measure on
the shifts a ∈ [0, )2 and angles θ ∈ [0, 2π), and notice that if we take any conformal
map f , then locally at each point f (x) ∈ f (Ω), in the push-forward of the average
we will still see the uniform distribution on the shifted and rotated |f 0 (x)|-boxes (or
rather almost-boxes). (For any given pair (a, θ), the a-shifted θ-rotated |f 0 (x1 )|-box
at some point f (x1 ) will come from a differently shifted and rotated -grid than the
(a, θ)-moved |f 0 (x2 )|-box at some other point f (x2 ), since the local rotation and shift
given by f is different at f (x1 ) and f (x2 ); however, the overall distributions are still
uniform at each point.) Therefore, the map f changes this average by the integral of
the right power of the local scaling |f 0 |. (To compare different scaled versions of a grid,
(1.4) is used again.) This will prove conformal covariance.
    Finally, what survives for other lattices, say, critical bond percolation on Z2 ?
Since the Russo-Seymour-Welsh technology works, all ingredients remain valid that do
not use the uniqueness and conformal invariance of the percolation scaling limit: the
basic topology and measurability results for the quad-crossing space (HΩ , TΩ ), the tight-
ness and moment estimates for the normalized counting measures, and the separation of
interfaces phenomena and the coupling results. (See Remark 3.5 for a tiny issue to han-
dle.) Therefore, we can still prove that whenever the scaling limit of static percolation
exists along a subsequence {ηk }∞k=1 , then the scaling limit of the normalized measures
also exists along that subsequence. Then we conclude in [GPS13a] that the dynamical
and near-critical percolation scaling limits also exist along the same subsequence and
are Markov processes. Note that the mere existence of subsequential scaling limits for
these processes would follow from the compactness of (HΩ , TΩ ), but the possibility of
using the same subsequence that already worked for the static scaling limit, and the
Markovianity of the limit are highly non-trivial.

written up in [DS11], to Vincent Beffara and Chuck Newman for explaining that the
results of [CN06] imply the uniqueness of the quad-crossing scaling limit, and to Asaf
Nachmias for encouraging us to include the statement about the rotational invariance
of the two-point connectivity function. We also thank René Conijn, Demeter Kiss, and
Alan Hammond for very useful comments on the manuscript, and Vincent Beffara for

the simulation pictures. A large part of the work was done while all authors were at

2     Arms, quads and loops
2.1    Notation and basics
Recall that we can consider site percolation on ηT as a two-coloring of the faces of the
hexagonal lattice, and hence of the plane (with edges shared by two differently colored
faces having both colors. In this context, we will use the words “hexagon”, “site”
and “point” interchangeably. We assume that the reader is familiar with the basics
of discrete critical planar percolation: the FKG-inequality, the Russo-Seymour-Welsh
(RSW) technology, and the mono- and polychromatic k-arm events. See [Wer07].
    We will use the multi-arm events and probabilities in several different versions. First
of all, αkη (r, R) will denote the probability that there are k arms, not all of the same
color when k > 1, connecting the two boundary pieces of the annulus A(r, R) = BR \Br ,
where Br will denote the square of Euclidean radius r (hence sidelength 2r). Of course,
there is a small problem with this definition: the exact set of hexagons intersecting this
annulus depends on where the center of the two squares is compared to the discrete
lattice. For a while, the precise definition will not matter, as long as it is fixed; say, the
center of the squares is the center of a hexagon. Later this will matter more, at which
point we will refine the definition. The notation αkη (η, R), for k ≤ 6, will always denote
the k-arm probability from a single site to radius R. Omitting the superscript η will
either mean (depending on the context) that we are talking about the continuum SLE6
quantity αk (r, R) = limη→0 αkη (r, R), or that it does not matter whether one uses the
continuum or the discrete quantity. There will be several more versions of the four-arm
event later on; see, for instance, Subsection 4.5.
    A well-known important property of k-arm probabilities is quasi-multiplicativity:

                ck αk (r1 , r2 ) αk (r2 , r3 ) ≤ αk (r1 , r3 ) ≤ αk (r1 , r2 ) αk (r2 , r3 ) ,

for some absolute constant ck > 0. For k = 1 this is easy from RSW and FKG, for k ≥ 2
it requires the (weak) separation of interfaces technology; see [Kes87, SSt10, Nol08].

2.2    The quad-crossing topology
We now define what we mean by the scaling limit of critical percolation. We will work
with the setup introduced in [SSm11], which describes the scaling limit using “left-
right” crossing events in generalized quadrilaterals. For completeness, we review
the basic definitions and results below. There are alternative setups that might work
equally well, even if we felt that using crossing events is the most practical one for
our purposes: Aizenman [Aiz96] suggested using the set of all open paths, Camia

                                                     15
and Newman [CN06] defined the scaling limit as the set of all interface loops, and
Sheffield defined a branching SLE tree [She09], which should be the limit of discrete
exploration trees in all models where the interfaces converge to SLEs. As pointed out
in [SSm11], where there is a discussion of several more possible definitions, it is a priori
highly non-trivial to prove that all these different notions contain the same relevant
information (i.e., that they are measurable with respect to each other). Nevertheless,
as we will explain in Subsection 2.3, the results of [CN06] imply that the quad-crossing
scaling limit is a function of the Camia-Newman scaling limit, while Subsection 2.4 is
concerned with what objects can be expressed in the quad-crossing limit. (We also
have a proof that the quad-topology is measurable with respect to the branching SLE6
tree, but that is more cumbersome than using the continuum loop ensemble, especially
that [CN06] has already established the uniqueness and several properties of the latter,
hence we have not written up that proof.)
    Let D ⊂ Ĉ = C ∪ {∞} be open. A quad in the domain D can be considered as a
homeomorphism Q from [0, 1]2 into D. The space of all quads in D, denoted by QD , can
be equipped with the following metric: dQ (Q1 , Q2 ) := inf φ supz∈∂[0,1]2 |Q1 (z)−Q2 (φ(z))|,
where the infimum is over all homeomorphisms φ : [0, 1]2 −→ [0, 1]2 which preserve the
4 corners of the square. A crossing of a quad Q is a connected closed subset of
[Q] := Q([0, 1]2 ) that intersects both ∂1 Q = Q({0} × [0, 1]) and ∂3 Q = Q({1} × [0, 1]).
    From the point of view of crossings, there is a natural partial order on QD : we write
Q1 ≤ Q2 if any crossing of Q2 contains a crossing of Q1 . See Figure 2.1. Furthermore,
we write Q1 < Q2 if there are open neighborhoods Ni of Qi (in the uniform metric) such
that N1 ≤ N2 holds for any Ni ∈ Ni . A subset S ⊂ QD is called hereditary if whenever
Q ∈ S and Q0 ∈ QD satisfies Q0 < Q, we also have Q0 ∈ S. The collection of all closed
hereditary subsets of QD will be denoted by HD . Any discrete percolation configuration
ωη of mesh η > 0, considered as a union of the topologically closed percolation-wise
open hexagons in the plane, naturally defines an element S(ωη ) of HD : the set of all
quads for which ωη contains a crossing. Thus, in particular, critical percolation induces
a probability measure on HD , which will be denoted by Pη . Note that since each quad
is closed in D and the elements of HD are closed hereditary sets, crossings of a quad
Q are allowed to use the boundary ∂Q.


                                                               Q2




                                     Q1

                            Figure 2.1: Two quads, Q1 ≤ Q2 .


                                             16
    Hereditary subsets can be thought of as Dedekind cuts in the setting of partially
ordered sets (instead of totally ordered sets, as usual). It can be therefore hoped that by
introducing a natural topology, HD can be made into a compact metric space. Indeed,
let us consider the following subsets of HD . For any Q ∈ QD , let Q := {S ∈ HD :
Q ∈ S}, and for any open U ⊂ QD , let U := {S ∈ HD : S ∩ U = ∅}. Observe that it
is natural to declare the sets cU to be open, and (since the quads themselves are closed
in D) the sets Q to be closed. Therefore, we define TD to be the minimal topology
that contains every cQ and cU as open sets. It is proved in [SSm11, Theorem 3.10]
that for any nonempty open D, the topological space (HD , TD ) is compact, Hausdorff,
and metrizable. Furthermore, for any dense Q0 ⊂ QD , the events { Q : Q ∈ Q0 }
generate the Borel σ-field of HD . Now, since Borel probability measures on a compact
metric space are always tight, we have subsequential scaling limits of Pη on HC , as
ηk → 0, denoted by P0 = P0 ({ηk }). It is proved in [SSm11, Corollary 5.2] that, for
any subsequential limit P0 , and any finite collection of events Q and cQ , the joint
probabilities converge along the subsequence; the main reason is that the boundary of
the joint event can be shown to have zero measure under P0 , so the weak convergence
of the measures Pηk to P0 is good enough.
    Of course, as explained carefully in [SSm11], the choice of the space HD (or any
other setup for the scaling limit) already poses restrictions on what events one can work
with. Note, for instance, that A := {∃ neighborhood U of the origin 0 ∈ C s.t. all quads
Q ⊂ U are crossed} is clearly in the Borel σ-field of (HD , TD ), and it is easy to see that
P0 [A] = 0 under any limit P0 , but if the sequence of η-lattices is such that 0 is always
the center of a hexagonal tile, then Pη [A] = 1/2. (The above machinery breaks down
because the boundary of the event A has positive, or in fact, full measure under P0 .)
Similarly, one can talk about the Borel-measurable event Mη in (HD , TD ) that counts
whether there are more open than closed η-hexagons in the percolation configuration
ωη in D, but there is no good candidate for such an event that would be non-trivial
under P0 . (And there is good reason for this failure: it is proved in [BKS99, Section 4]
that crossing events are asymptotically independent from majority events.) Therefore,
it is important to know that for a lot of natural events such problems do not occur.
This will be the goal of Subsection 2.4 below.
    As mentioned above, (HD , TD ) is a compact metrizable topological space. Unfor-
tunately, we have not found a natural explicit metric that would yield this topology.
However, in Subsection 2.4 below, it will be important to understand well what it means
for two configurations to be close to each other. To this end, we will now define an
explicit countable subbase of TD .
Definition 2.1. (A dyadic family of quads) For any k ≥ 1, let (Qkn )1≤n≤Nk be the family
of all quads which are polygonal quads in D ∩ 2−k Z2 , i.e., their boundary ∂Qkn consists
of edges of D ∩ 2−k Z2 and the four marked vertices are vertices of D ∩ 2−k Z2 . (For fixed
k, there are finitely many such quads since the domain D is assumed to be bounded).
We will denote by Qk = QkD this family of quads. Notice that Qk ⊂ Qk+1 .


                                            17
    Clearly, the family QN := k Qk is dense in the space of quads (QD , dQ ). Thus, as
                               S
mentioned above, the events { Q : Q ∈ QN } generate the Borel σ-field of HD .
    In order to use the open sets of the form cU , where U is an open set of QD , we
will associate to each Q ∈ Qk , (k ≥ 1), the open set Q̂k := BdQ (Q, 2−k−10 ), and with a
slight abuse of notation, we will write cQ̂ for the open set cQ̂ .

we have chosen here to relax cQ into cQ̄ . This choice makes the definition and hence
the forthcoming proofs more symmetric.
Remark 2.4. Let us point out that for any ω ∈ H and any k ≥ 0, we have that
ω ∈ Ok+1 (ω) ⊂ Ok (ω). Hence the finite coverings C k := {Ok (ω) : ω ∈ H } are finer
and finer as k → ∞.
   We will use this family of neighbourhoods through the following lemma.

there exists a function r : N+ −→ R+ such that, for any k ≥ 1 and any ω, ω 0 ∈ H , if
dH (ω, ω 0 ) ≤ r(k), then ω 0 ∈ Ok (ω) and ω ∈ Ok (ω 0 ).
    In words, if ω and ω 0 are sufficiently close (r(k)-close) to each other, then (up to
small perturbations of 2−k−10 ) they have the same crossings for all quads in Qk .

2.3    Uniqueness of the quad-crossing percolation limit
In [SSm11], only subsequential limits limk→∞ Pηk = P0 ({ηk }) are considered. As ex-
plained in the introduction, it is crucial for us to know that there is a unique and
conformally invariant scaling limit in this quad-crossing space. It turns out that this


                                                19
uniqueness property can be recovered from another notion of the scaling limit of per-
colation: the continuum non-simple loop ensemble of [CN06]. The point of view,
or rather the topology considered in [CN06] is quite different from the approach in
[SSm11]. Instead of keeping track of the crossing events for quads, one keeps track
of all the interface loops (that lie between some open cluster and some closed one).
The loops are oriented depending whether their inside is open or not. To a discrete
percolation configuration ωη on ηT, one thus associates a collection of oriented loops
{`i (ωη )}i∈N .
     Let us briefly describe what is the topology of convergence in [CN06]. First of all,
the loops correspond here to continuous maps from the circle to the plane C. They
are identified up to reparametrization by homeomorphisms of the circle with positive
winding. Since we want to consider percolation configurations in the whole plane, it is
convenient to compactify C as usual into C ∪ {∞} ≃ S2 . Let dS2 be the induced metric
on C ∪ {∞}.
     We now equip the space L of such loops with the following (pseudo-)distance

                           dL (`, `0 ) := inf sup dS2 `(t), `0 (φ(t)) ,
                                                                     
                                           φ t∈R/Z


where the infimum is taken over all homeomorphisms of the circle which have positive
winding (recall that loops are oriented).
   Now, let L be the space of countable collections of loops in L. As mentioned above,
any discrete percolation configuration ωη gives rise to an element of L. We consider the
Hausdorff topology on L induced by dL . Namely if c, c0 ∈ L, let

  dL (c, c0 ) := inf{ > 0 : ∀ ` ∈ c ∃ `0 ∈ c0 and ∀ `0 ∈ c0 ∃ ` ∈ c such that dL (`, `0 ) ≤ } .

    In [CN06], the following theorem is shown:
Theorem 2.6 ([CN06]). Let ωη be a critical percolation configuration on the rescaled
triangular grid ηT (on the whole plane). The random configuration ωη considered as
a random element ιη in L converges in law, under the topology induced by dL , to a
continuum percolation ι ∈ L.
    Let PL0 denote the law of the above continuum percolation ι ∈ L. Several properties
of this scaling limit ι are established; most importantly:
Proposition 2.7 (“finite chaining”, [CN06], third item in Theorem 2). Almost surely
(under PL0 ), for any pair of loops `, `0 ∈ ι, there is a finite set a loops `0 = `, `1 , . . . , `k =
`0 in ι, such that for all j ∈ [1, k], `i−1 ∩ `i 6= ∅.
   We will not enter in more details here, but, using the fact that at the scaling limit
there are no 6-arms events, it is easy to see that almost surely if `, `0 ∈ ι touch each
other and have the same orientation, then one loop cannot lie “inside” the other one.
Conversely, if two loops of different orientations touch each other, then one has to be

                                                 20
“inside” the other one. The meaning of “inside” needs some care here, since on a
typical loop there are inside “fjords” and exterior ones. See [CN06] for more details.
This condition implies a parity constraint on the above finite chaining property.
Uniqueness of the scaling limit under the quad-crossing topology. To establish
the uniqueness, it is enough to characterize uniquely the subsequential scaling limits
P0 . To achieve this, one has to prove that for any finite set of quads Q1 , Q2 , . . . , Qp ,
the joint law of the crossing events Q1 (ωη ), . . . , Qp (ωη ) converges in law to a unique
random p-vector. We can restrict ourselves to piecewise smooth quads, since they form
a dense family in QC . Notice that the p = 1 case corresponds to Cardy’s formula (and
thus is not known on Z2 ). If we had at our disposal a joint Cardy’s formula, we would
be done. For example, Watts’ formula, proved in [Dub06, SW11], is a special case of
p = 2. Such a general Cardy’s fomula is not known, but fortunately we do not need an
explicit formula here — we just need to show that the joint laws converge. Let us fix
our finite set of quads Q1 , Q2 , . . . , Qp , and consider percolation configurations ωη with
mesh η → 0. Viewed as sets of loops, they converge to a continuum set of loops ι ∼ PL0 .
For any j ∈ [1, p], as is well-known, the crossing event Qj (ωη ) can be recovered from
the discrete exploration path starting at one of the 4 corners of Qj . It is known that
such an exploration path converges towards an SLE6 curve in Qj . Now the loops in
ι are made of SLE6 curves, hence at first sight one seems to be in good shape. The
trouble is that these SLE6 curves sit in the plane and do not see ∂Qj . Therefore, the
continuum exploration path which would give us whether Qj is satisfied or not is made
of many pieces of SLE6 loops coming from ι. Thus it is not a priori clear that Qj is
measurable with respect to ι. The answer to this question is provided in [CN06]; the
proof (using the finite chaining lemma and the parity condition mentioned above) can
be found right after Theorem 7 in [CN06]:
Proposition 2.8. Let (Q, a, b, c, d) be a piece-wise smooth quad in the plane. Let ωη
be a sequence of percolation configurations which converge pointwise (for dL ) towards
ι ∼ PL0 . (This can be done using Skorokhod representation theorem). The exploration
paths γη from a to b converge pointwise (for the Hausdorff topology) to an SLE6 curve
γ from a to b which can be a.s. recovered from ι in the sense that γ = γ(ι) can be
constructed as a measurable function of ι.
    Hence, for each quad Qj , simultaneously, one can extract from the continuum per-
colation ι ∼ PL0 an exploration path γj which almost surely tells us about the crossing
event in Qj . (Only almost surely, since it could happen, for example, that γj inter-
sects one side at just a single point, in which case Qj could be crossed in some of the
ωη configurations and not crossed in others, so we would not get convergence of the
crossing events, or could get the wrong limit. But this happens only with probability
zero, due to the half-plane 3-arm event having exponent larger than 1.) This shows the
uniqueness of the quad-crossing limit.
Conformal invariance of the scaling limit under the quad-crossing topology.
The previous paragraph can be rephrased as follows: the continuum limit ω (under the

                                             21
quad topology [SSm11]) is a measurable function of the continuum limit ι (under the
above topology [CN06]). The conformal invariance of ι is provided by Theorem 7 in
[CN06]. In this section, we introduced the scaling limit ι only in the plane C, but it
can be defined for simply connected domains as well. See [CN06] for more details. If
ι is a continuum percolation in some domain Ω and f : Ω −→ Ω̃ is a conformal map,
then ι̃ := f (ι) (where each loop ` in ι is mapped conformally to a loop f (`) in ι̃) has
the law of a continuum percolation in Ω̃. This conformal invariance together with the
above discussion imply that if ω is a scaling limit for (HΩ , TΩ ), then ω̃ := f (ω) (defined
by f (Q) (ω̃) := Q (ω) for a dense family of quads Q ⊂ Ω) has the law of a continuum
percolation for (HΩ̃ , TΩ̃ ). This type of invariance will be crucial in Section 6.

2.4    The limit of arm events
We need to define the usual arm events in a way that makes them measurable in the
Borel σ-field of the quad-crossing topology TD and as amenable as possible for proving
the convergence of their probabilities as η → 0. Namely, for any topological annulus
A ⊂ D with piecewise smooth inner and outer boundary      pieces ∂1 A and ∂2 A, we define
the alternating 4-arm event in A as A4 = δ>0 A4 , where Aδ4 is the existence of
                                                        δ
                                                 S
quads Qi ⊂ D, i = 1, 2, 3, 4, with the following properties (see Figure 2.4):

  (i) Q1 and Q3 are disjoint and are at distance at least δ from each other; the same
      for Q2 and Q4 ;

 (ii) for i ∈ {1, 3}, the sides Qi ({0} × [0, 1]) lie inside ∂1 A and the sides Qi ({1} × [0, 1])
      lie outside ∂2 A; for i ∈ {2, 4}, the sides Qi ([0, 1] × {0}) lie inside ∂1 A and the
      sides Qi ([0, 1] × {1}) lie outside ∂2 A; all these sides are at distance at least δ from
      the annulus A and from the other Qj ’s;

(iii) the four quads are ordered cyclically around A according to their indices;

 (iv) For i ∈ {1, 3}, we have ω ∈ Qi , while for i ∈ {2, 4}, we have ω ∈ cQi . In plain
      words, the quads Q1 , Q3 are crossed, while the quads Q2 , Q4 are dual crossed
      between the boundary pieces of A (with a margin δ of safety).

   The definitions of general (mono- or polychromatic) k-arm events in A are of
course analogous: for arms of the same color we require the corresponding quads to
be completely disjoint, and we still require all the boundary pieces lying outside the
annulus A to be disjoint.

Lemma 2.9. Let A ⊂ D be a piecewise smooth topological annulus (with finitely many
non-smooth boundary points). Then the 1-arm, any polychromatic 2- and 3-arm, the
alternating 4-arm and any polychromatic 6-arm event in A, denoted by A1 , A2 , A3 , A4
and A6 , respectively, are measurable w.r.t. the scaling limit of critical percolation in D,

and limη→0 Pη [Ai ] = P0 [Ai ]. Moreover, in any coupling of the measures {Pη } and P0
on (HD , TD ) in which ωη → ω a.s. as η → 0, we have
                                             

Proof. Using a countable dense subset of QD , it is clear that Ai is in the Borel
σ-field of (HD , TD ). In fact, it is also easy to see that it is an open set. It fol-
lows
   that, in any coupling ωη → ω, we have lim inf η→0 11Ai (ωη ) ≥ 11Ai (ω) and hence
P {ω ∈ Ai } \ {ωη ∈ Ai } → 0. The nontrivial direction is that
                                                    

The main step will be to prove that for each i = 1, 2, 3, 4, 6 there exists a function
i : [0, 1] −→ [0, 1] with limδ→0 i (δ) = 0 such that

                        Pη [Aδi | Ai ] > 1 − i (δ)   for all η > 0 ,                 (2.3)

so that we can detect the i arms with quads satisfying the δ-disjointness criteria with
a high probability that does not depend on the mesh η.
    Let us start with the i = 4 case. If we have A4 in ωη , then choose 4 alternating
arms arbitrarily, consider their connected components (in their own color), and take
the counterclockwisemost simple path in each component that connects ∂1 A to ∂2 A,
denoted by γi , i = 1, 2, 3, 4, in counterclockwise order. Clearly, if some γi and γi+2 come
δ-close to each other somewhere inside A, at distance δ 0 from the closer boundary piece
∂i A, then we have a polychromatic 7-arm event from that δ-ball to distance δ 0 , and,
assuming that the boundary is smooth here in a neighbourhood of macroscopic size,
we have a half-plane 4-arm event from the 2δ 0 -neighborhood of ∂i A to a distance of
unit order. See Figure 2.4. Around points of non-smoothness at the boundary, possibly
with an inner angle as large as 2π, we have to consider the 4-arm event in the “half-
plane squared”, giving the approximate square root of the half-plane probability on

                                              23
ηT (by conformal invariance). Using that the boundary is composed of finitely many
smooth pieces, we get that the above δ-closenessevent happens with probability at
most O δ −2 α7 (δ, 1) + δ −1 α4+ (δ, 1) + α4+ (δ, 1)1/2+o(1) on ηT.
