Figure 2.4: Convergence for A4 . Closeness implies here a 7-arm whole plane event from
radius δ to δ 0 , and a 4-arm half-plane event from 2δ 0 to a unit order.

    Furthermore, if the endpoints of any two of our four arms come δ-close on a smooth
part of ∂i A, then we have a half-plane 3-arm event from a δ-ball on that ∂i A to a
distance of unit order, or, at a non-smooth boundary point, a 3-arm event in the half-
plane squared, in the worst case. So, this        δ-closeness event happens with probability
               −1 +              +      1/2+o(1)
at most O δ α3 (δ, 1) + α3 (δ, 1)                 .
    Finally, since we want our four quads to overhang the boundary pieces ∂1 A and ∂2 A,
we need to continue our four arms to an additional distance δ at each end. This can be
done unless we are stopped by a crossing of the opposite colour, which, together with
our arm, gives a 3-arm event at the boundary, so the probability is bounded again by
O δ −1 α3+ (δ, 1) + α3+ (δ, 1)1/2+o(1) .
    In summary, using the 7-arm probability in the plane (exponent > 2) and the 3-arm
probabilities in the half-plane and the whole plane (exponent = 2 and > 0, respectively),
we get that, with probability 1 − O(δ γ ), γ > 0, none of the above δ-closeness events
happen, hence we can clearly find the four quads required, and we are done.
    (Note that if some γi and γi+1 come close to each other, then we get only a poly-
chromatic 5-arm event, which still happens sometimes in the annulus. That is why we
allow neighbouring quads to overlap in our definition of Aδi .)



                                             24
    Assume now that A3 holds in ωη ; say, there are two disjoint closed arms and one
open. Viewed from the given open arm o, take the clockwisemost and counterclock-
wisemost simple closed arms connecting ∂1 A to ∂2 A, denoted by c1 and c2 . If we take
any xi on each ci , then there is a open path o0 = o0 (x1 , x2 ) connecting them. If c1 and
c2 come δ-close to each other without sandwiching o, with some points xi on ci , then
we get a 6-arm event around the pair x1 , x2 : four closed arms given by c1 and c2 , and
two open arms given by o0 . If c1 and c2 come δ-close to each other while sandwiching
o, then we have 6 arms given by c1 , c2 and o. Of course, if the points of closeness are
close to either boundary piece ∂i A, then we have to consider half-plane 3-arm events,
as well. Altogether, we get that, with good probability, none of these δ-closeness events
happen, moreover, just as for A4 , we can extend the crossings to additional distances
δ at the ends, and we are done.
   The case of A6 clearly follows from the combination of the above arguments for A3
and A4 .

                                     γ1c
                                                         γ2c        ∂2 A




                                           γ1    γ2

                                                      ∂1 A




Figure 2.5: Convergence for A2 . How to avoid δ-closeness despite a 5-arm event around
a δ-ball produced by γ1o and γ2c .

    Now assume that A2 holds; then there are at least two interfaces from ∂1 A to ∂2 A.
Condition on the set of all the interfaces: its cardinality is a positive even number.
If there are at least 4 interfaces, then also A4 holds, so, by our above result, we can
detect even four arms, thus did not lose any probability in the scaling limit. Therefore,
we may assume that there are exactly two interfaces, denoted by γ1 and γ2 . Let the
right (clockwise) side of γ1 and the left (counterclockwise) side of γ2 be the open sides.
Denote the outer boundaries of the two γi ’s, two open and two closed simple paths, by

                                                25
γ1c , γ1o , γ2o , γ2c , in the clockwise order. Of course, γ1o and γ2o do not have to be disjoint
from each other at all, and the same for the γic ’s. Consider now γ1o and γ2c . It is possible
that these two paths come very close to each other by sandwiching γ2 : away from the
boundaries ∂i A this requires a 5-arm event, which has exponent 2. More precisely,
the expected number of 5-arm events from a grid of δ-boxes to unit distance is finite
and positive, uniformly in the mesh η, see [Wer07, First exercise sheet]; therefore, the
number of these 5-arm δ-closeness events (for any fixed δ) is tight in η. Denote these
δ-balls by B1 , . . . , Bt , t = t(δ, η). We want to find a closed arm that goes around these
balls. For this, consider γ1c : it is unlikely that it comes very close to any of these balls
(in particular, that it intersects any of them), since that would produce already a 6-arm
event by bringing in an extra open arm (coming from the open side of γ1 ). So, around
any of the Bj , there is a region of “macroscopic radius” that is bordered by the two
closed arms given by γ2c and by γ1c . In this region between γ1c and γ2c that does not contain
the interfaces γi , all the information that we have about the percolation configuration
is that there is no open arm from ∂1 A to ∂2 A. This is a monotone increasing event
for “closed”, hence, by the FKG inequality, we can apply RSW in consecutive disjoint
annuli around Bj to produce a closed shortcut between the two closed arms given by
γ1c . Since the number t(δ, η) of the 5-arm balls that we need to go around is tight in
η, with large probability we can construct a closed arm that does not come δ-close to
γ1o , anywhere far from the boundaries ∂i A. As usual, boundary closeness can easily be
excluded using the 3-arm half-plane event.




                                         ∂2 A                               δ


                                                                        F


                         ∂1 A




Figure 2.6: Convergence for A1 . The left picture shows how to find an open (red) simple
arm using the radial exploration process. The right picture shows a typical way how a
δ-almost self-touch of that open simple arm would imply a 6-arm event from radius δ.

    For A1 , there is a new difficulty compared to the previous cases: if there is no
closed crossing in A, i.e., there is an open circuit, then things like the “clockwisemost
simple path in the component of the open crossing” are not well-defined. So, let us

                                                26
take a radial exploration interface: start from the inner boundary ∂1 A, with open
hexagons on the right, closed hexagons on the left of the interface. If the interface
makes a clockwise loop around ∂1 A, then we have discovered a closed circuit, so there
is no open crossing. Whenever the interface makes a counterclockwise loop around ∂1 A,
let us pretend that the previously visited open hexagon which the interface has just
bumped into was closed, and continue the exploration. After the first such forced turn,
the interface can bump into itself not only because of counterclockwise loops around
∂1 A, but also because of the recolored hexagons; nevertheless, the rule for recoloring
hexagons remains the same. This interface reaches ∂2 A if and only if there is an open
crossing. Given this event, erase chronologically the counterclockwise loops around ∂1 A
it has completed. The resulting interface has an open (non-simple) crossing path on
its right, without loops around ∂1 A. Taking the right (clockwise) boundary of it, we
get a simple open path. See the left picture on Figure 2.6. We now claim that the
probability that this path comes to δ-close to itself (after a macroscopic detour) goes to
0 as δ → 0, uniformly in η, hence it does not happen in the scaling limit. In particular,
our open simple path does not make loops around ∂1 A in the scaling limit, and hence
we can detect it with the event of crossing a quad.
    We still need to prove the claim. If our simple open path was the outer boundary
of a chordal exploration path, then coming δ-close would produce a 6-arm event from
radius δ to order 1, and we would be done. Now the exploration path can also go
around ∂1 A, and come δ-close to itself from the other side. This would again cause a
6-arm event. See the right picture of Figure 2.6. However, because of the forced turns
(denoted by F on the same picture), some of the closed arms among those 6 arms might
be faulty: open hexagons appear at the forced turns, usually building large pieces of
mixed color arms that we pretended to be closed. (For instance, on the left picture of
Figure 2.6, we have four faulty hexagons next to each other.) What saves us is that the
first time a closed arm emanating from a ball of δ-closeness reaches a faulty hexagon (on
either side of a faulty piece of an arm), there are at least two additional genuine arms
emanating from that neighbourhood (since we have to produce the faulty hexagon, by
the radial exploration path touching itself). Combining with the fact that the number
of macroscopically different faulty places is tight as η → 0 (because they imply 5-arm
events), one gets that these faulty places do not help noticeably our open path to come
δ-close to itself. This finishes the proof of (2.3).
   The point of (2.3) is that if Aδi (ω) holds for some ω ∈ H and δ > 0, and if we
choose k such that 2−k < δ/210 , then any ω 0 ∈ Ok (ω) will clearly satisfy Ai , as well.
Thus, (2.3) implies that, for all η > 0,

                  Pη Ai (ω 0 ) for all ω 0 ∈ Ok (ω) Ai (ω) > 1 − i (δ) .
                                                         
                                                                                    (2.4)




                                           27
Now, take a coupling in which ωη → ω almost surely. By Lemma 2.5, for η = η(k, δ)
small enough, we have P ω ∈ Ok (ωη ) > 1 − i (δ). Therefore,
                                                                 
        P {ωη ∈ Ai } \ {ω ∈ Ai } ≤ P ωη ∈ Ai , ω ∈ Ok (ωη ), ω 6∈ Ai + i (δ)
                                  ≤ 2 i (δ) ,  using (2.4) .

By taking δ → 0, we obtain (2.2), finishing the proof of the lemma.
    For future reference, let us reiterate that the proof of Lemma 2.9 implies the follow-
ing quantitative bound on how close the event Aδ4 is to the event A4 .

Corollary 2.10. On ηT, for any piecewise smooth annulus A and any γ < 1, there is
a constant c = cA,γ > 0 such that, for any δ > 0:

                                P Aδ4 A4 ≥ 1 − c δ γ .
                                         


It is easy to see that the same result holds on Z2 , as well, only with some undetermined
exponent γ > 0 instead of it being arbitrarily close to 1.

Remark 2.11. The above proofs clearly apply also to the case when the arms have to
end at prescribed arcs on one or both of the boundaries ∂i A.
Remark 2.12. As mentioned above, [SSm11, Corollary 5.2] proved the k → ∞ con-
vergence of the Pηk -probability of the intersection of any finite set of quad crossing
and non-crossing events, where {ηk } is a subsequence for which the limit P0 ({η}) in
(HD , TD ) exists. Therefore, the proof of the above lemma, together with the uniqueness
of the quad-crossing limit, imply the convergence of the joint Pη -distribution of any
finite set of macroscopic arm events, and the convergence in probability of the joint
indicator in any coupling where ωη → ω as η → 0; the main point is that, in the scaling
limit, the 6-arm and half-plane 3-arm events do not occur anywhere in the finite set
of annuli, hence the convergence of quad crossings and non-crossings really measures
what we want.

   Expressing arm events using the quad-crossing topology T is a natural first step to-
wards proving that other notions of the percolation scaling limit are measurable w.r.t. T .
For instance, we immediately get the following partial result towards extracting an SLE6
from the quad-crossing scaling limit.

Corollary 2.13. In a smooth domain Ω with boundary points a, b ∈ Ω, the joint law
(ωη , γη ) of the discrete quad-crossing configuration ωη and the exploration path trace γη
from aη to bη (where aη → a and bη → b) converges to a coupling (ω, γ), where ω is a
percolation quad-crossing scaling limit and γ is the trace of a chordal SLE6 from a to
b that is a function of ω. The topology for the convergence of γη to γ is the Hausdorff
distance of closed sets in Ω.


                                            28
Proof. Note that for any  > 0, a closed -box Q inside Ω is touched by the exploration
path γη iff there are two arms from ∂Q to the boundary arcs ab and ba, in the appropriate
colors. Consider any finite covering of Ω by -boxes. By Remarks 2.11 and 2.12 applied
to the 2-arm events from these small -boxes to the smooth boundary arcs ab and ba,
and by the convergence in law of the exploration path γη to a chordal SLE6 curve γ (see
Subsection 5.3 below), the set of -boxes touched by γη converges a.s., in any coupling
with γη → γ, to the set of -boxes touched by γ, and this set is measurable w.r.t. the
quad-crossing topology T . Taking a decreasing intersection of these compact sets as
 → 0, we get the measurability of the trace of the SLE6 path γ.
    However, this convergence of the closed sets γη to γ is weaker than what one would
really want for curves that naturally have their points ordered. “Cutting” the closed
set γ into a continuous increasing family in such a way that it gives the right curve
would require work. So, the following question remains. See Subsection 5.3 for some
related discussion.
Question 2.14. Is it the case that the chordal SLE6 curve is measurable with respect
to the quad-crossing continuum percolation ω inside (Ω, a, b)?
    Assuming a positive answer to Question 2.14, one could also try to do the measura-
bility of the Camia-Newman description of the full scaling limit using iterated chordal
SLE6 paths [CN06], but there is an additional issue here: the iterative process requires
running the SLE6 paths in domains with fractal boundary, while we required smooth
boundaries above.


3    Coupling argument
Let us consider some annulus A = A(u, v) of inner radius u and outer radius v > u.
Let ωη be a percolation configuration on the triangular grid of mesh η inside A. Call
Γ the set of percolation interfaces which cross A (it might be that there are no such
interfaces, in which case Γ = ∅). We will need to measure how well separated the
interfaces are on the inside boundary ∂1 A. For that purpose we define a measure of the
(interior) quality Q(ωη ) = Q(Γ) to be the least distance between the endpoints of Γ
on ∂1 A normalized by u. More precisely, if there are p ≥ 2 interfaces crossing A and if
x1 , . . . , xp denote the endpoints of these interfaces on ∂1 A, then we define
                                                1
                            Q(ωη ) = Q(Γ) =       inf |xk − xl |,
                                                u k6=l
where | · | denotes Euclidean distance. If Γ = ∅, we define Q(Γ) to be zero.
   We define similarly the exterior quality Q+ (ωη ) = Q+ (Γ) to be the least distance
between the endpoints of Γ on ∂2 A normalized by v (and set to be zero if there are
no such interfaces). For any α > 0, let T α (u, v) be the event that the quality Q(Γ) is
bigger than α; also, T+α (u, v) will denote the event that Q+ (Γ) > α.

                                           29
     For a square BR of radius R, we define a notion of faces around that square. Let
x1 , . . . , x4 be four distinct points on ∂BR chosen in a counterclockwise order. We will
adopt here cyclic notation, i.e., for any j ∈ Z, we have xj = xi if j ≡ i[4]. For any
i ∈ Z, let θi be a simple path of hexagons joining xi to xi+1 , i.e., a sequence of hexagons
h1 , . . . , hn such that hi and hj are neighbors if and only if |i − j| = 1. We assume
furthermore that there are no hexagons in θi which are entirely contained in the square
of radius R (they might still intersect ∂BR ) and that all the hexagons in θi are white
(=open) if i is odd and black (=closed) if i is even (the endpoints xi could be of either
colour). If a set of paths Θ = {θ1 , . . . , θ4 } satisfies the above conditions, Θ will be called
a configuration of faces with endpoints x1 , . . . , x4 . We define similarly the quality of a
configuration of faces Q(Θ) to be the least distance between the endpoints of the faces,
normalized by R.
     Let G(u, v) be the event that there exist 4 alternating arms from radius u to v and
there is no extra disjoint arm crossing A. In particular, on the event G(u, v), the set
of interfaces Γ consists of exactly 4 interfaces, and furthermore, any two consecutive
interfaces have to share at least one hexagon (if not, there would be at least 5 arms
from u to v). It is easy to see that on the event G(u, v), the 4 interfaces of Γ induce
a natural configuration of faces Θ = Θ(Γ) at radius u with same endpoints x1 , . . . , x4
as Γ. More precisely, if H is the set of all the hexagons neighboring the 4 interfaces in
Γ, then by the definition of G(u, v), the connected component of C \ H which contains
the center of the annulus A is a bounded domain; the set of hexagons which lie on the
boundary of this domain form the 4 faces of Θ. In what follows, when we condition on
the event G(u, v), we will often condition also on the configuration of faces Θ. (Notice
that, by definition, on the event G(u, v) we have Q(Γ) = Q(Θ)).
     If we are given a square of radius R and a configuration of faces Θ = {θ1 , . . . , θ4 }
around that square, D = DΘ will denote the bounded component of C \ Θ (this is a
finite set of η-hexagons). Let U = UΘ be the random variable which is set to be one
if there is an open crossing from θ1 to θ3 inside DΘ and 0 otherwise. For any radius
r < R, let AΘ (r, R) be the event that there are open arms from the box of radius r to
the open faces θ1 and θ3 and there are closed arms from r to the closed faces θ2 , θ4 (in
other words, if one starts 4 interfaces in DΘ at the endpoints of Θ at radius R, then
these interfaces go all the way to radius r).
     Let Q be the square of radius 1 around the origin. As a particular case of the above,
for any η < r < 1, we define A0 (r, 1) to be the event that there are open arms from
the square of radius r to the left and right edges of Q and there are closed arms from
r to the top and bottom edges of Q. Similarly, U0 will be the indicator function of a
left-right crossing in Q.

Proposition 3.1 (Coupling property). Let τ ∈ {0, 1}, and let A = A(r, R) be the
annulus centered around 0 with radii 100η < 10r < R ≤ 1. Assume we are given any
configuration of faces Θ = {θ1 , . . . , θ4 } around the square of radius R. Let νΘ be the
law of the percolation configuration inside DΘ conditioned on the events AΘ (r, R) and


                                               30
{UΘ = τ }.
    Let ν0 be the law of the percolation configuration in the square Q under the condi-
tioning that A0 (r, 1) and {U0 = 1} hold.
    There exists an absolute exponent k > 0 such that the following holds. If τ = 1, there
is a coupling of the conditional laws νΘ and ν0 so that with (conditional) probability at
least 1 − (r/R)k , the event G(r, R) is satisfied for both configurations, and the induced
faces at radius r, Θ(r) and Θ0 (r), are identical. If τ = 0, there is also such a coupling
except that the faces Θ(r) and Θ0 (r) are (with probability at least 1 − (r/R)k ) identical
but with reversed color (see Figure 3.1).




Figure 3.1: Successful coupling of νΘ and ν0 when UΘ = τ = 0: the two four-tuples of
interfaces induce the same configuration of faces at radius r, only with reversed colors.

Remark 3.2. The proposition also holds if the annulus A is not centered around the
origin, but there are issues here coming from the discrete lattice: indeed, the set of
η-hexagons intersecting a square S is not invariant under translations of the square S.
We will deal with this issue in the next section.
    The proof of this coupling property will rely on the very useful separation of in-
terfaces phenomenon, which has several versions in the literature, for several different
planar models (percolation, random walks, Gaussian free field, loop-erased random
walk). The following percolation lemma is essentially from [DS11], but, for complete-
ness, the proof of this exact version is included in Appendix A below, together with a
discussion of the general phenomenon.
Lemma 3.3 (Strong Separation Lemma). Let A = A(R1 , R2 ) be the annulus centered
around 0 with radii 100η < 10r < 2R1 < R2 . Assume we are given some configuration
of faces Θ = {θ1 , . . . , θ4 } around the square of radius R2 . Note that the initial quality
Q(Θ) might be arbitrarily small (it could be of order η, for example).

                                             31
    Let νΘ be the conditional law of the percolation configuration inside DΘ conditioned
on the event AΘ (r, R2 ), and let Γ = Γ(R1 ) be the four-tuple of interfaces in DΘ which
start at the four endpoints of Θ until they reach radius R1 .
    There is some absolute constant c > 0 such that
                     h          1             i     h         1i
                    P Q(Γ) >       AΘ (r, R2 ) = νΘ Q(Γ) >       > c.
                                4                             4
In other words, conditioned on the event AΘ (r, R2 ), interfaces which might be initially
very close to each other tend to quickly “separate”.
   If we further condition on {τ = 1} or {τ = 0}, the result is still valid (with possibly
a smaller absolute constant c).

We now use the following easy fact, which is part of the folklore, though we are not
aware of an explicit proof in the literature:
Lemma 3.4. In the annulus A = A(r, 2r), there is a uniformly positive probability to
have exactly 4 disjoint alternating arms crossing A, with the endpoints of the resulting
                                                                                   
4 interfaces on the two boundaries of A having quality at least 1/4. That is, P Ri > c
for an absolute constant c > 0.
Proof. Let us provide two proofs, the first using Reimer’s inequality [Rei00], the second
being longer, but completely elementary, hence having a chance to be generalizable to
other models, like the FK random cluster model.
    Let A be the event that there exist four alternating arms in A, with the addi-
tional property that the four interfaces given by the clockwise boundaries of the con-
nected monochromatic components of A containing these arms have well-separated
endpoints: their interior and exterior
                                         qualities are both at least 1/4. It is clear
from RSW techniques that P A > c1 > 0. Let B = {there is an arm (open or
closed) from ∂1 A to ∂2 A}. Then, by Reimer, P[AB] = P[polychromatic 5 arms
in A, four of them giving well-separated interfaces]≤ P[A] P[B]. But RSW implies
P[B c ] > c2 > 0, so we get P[A \ AB] = P[exactly 4 arms in A, giving well-separated
interfaces] > c2 P[A] > c1 c2 > 0, and we are done.
    For the elementary proof, we first show that in the square there is a uniformly
positive probability of the event that there is a left-right crossing but no two disjoint
ones (which is the same as having at least one pivotal open bit), with the additional
property that there are open arms from a pivotal bit to the left and right sides in
the horizontal middle one-third of the square, and there are closed arms to the top and
bottom sides in the vertical middle third. See the left hand picture of Figure 3.2. Let us
denote the central ninth of the square by C, and its neighbouring ninths by N, E, S, W ,
in the obvious manner. Finally, let the left third of C be CW , the right third CE , and
the middle third CC .
    By RSW, there is a positive probability for a left-right open crossing in C; the
uppermost such crossing can be found by running an exploration process from the
upper left corner to the upper right corner of C, with open bits on the right (below the
interface), closed bits on the left. So, the lower boundary of the set of explored bits
is all open, the upper boundary is all closed, except the bits on the boundary of C,
where they are unexplored (the interface only pretended that they satisfy the suitable
boundary conditions). Furthermore, all bits beyond these boundaries are unexplored,
hence unbiased. So, by RSW, with positive probability we get a closed path in CC ∪ N
connecting the upper side of the large square to the upper (closed) boundary of the

                                           34
interface, and another closed path in CC ∪ S from the lower side of the large square to
the lower (open) boundary of the interface. Where this closed arm hits the open side of
the interface will be the pivotal we are looking for. Then, again by RSW, with positive
probability there is an open path inside W ∪ CW connecting the left side of the large
square to the open side of the interface, and another open path in CE ∪ E connecting
the interface to the right side of the square. This finishes the construction for our first
claim.



                    N



     W                            E
              CW C C CE


                    S



Figure 3.2: Constructing exactly four arms in an annulus, in a way that gives well-
separated interfaces.

    Now let us divide the annulus A(r, 2r) into four congruent sectors (N , E, S, W ),
and each sector into nine pieces, as shown on the right hand picture of Figure 3.2. All
the sectors and the pieces are nice quads, so we can translate our previous claim to
get the following: with positive probability, each of the odd sectors (N, S) contains
a pivotal bit for an open crossing between the sides of the quad that are part of the
annulus boundaries, each of the even sectors (W, E) contain a pivotal bit for a closed
crossing between the sides that are part of the annulus boundaries, and all the open
and closed arms emanating from these pivotals are contained in the middle pieces of
their sectors. Then, using RSW and FKG, we can glue together these arms such that
we get an open circuit in A(r, 2r) with just two closed bits on it: our closed pivotals in
the sectors W, E; and can also get a closed circuit with just two open bits on it: our
open pivotals in N, S. Finally, we can have additional connections in some of the pieces
to ensure that the resulting four interfaces are well-separated; see again the picture. All
of this happens with a uniformly positive probability, hence the proof is complete.

Proof of Proposition 3.1, continued. Summarizing what is above: we proved that
at any scale 0 ≤ i < N = blog8 ( Rr )c, if the event Wi holds (which under νΘ ⊗ ν0 holds


                                            35
with positive probability), then there is some universal constant c > 0 such that

                           P Ri AΘi (r, ri ), UΘi = τ, Θi ≥ c ,
                                                        
                                                                                         (3.3)
and
                           P Ri AΘi0 (r, ri ), UΘi0 = 1, Θi0 ≥ c .
                                                           
                                                                                         (3.4)

     We now have the tools which enable us to construct the coupling between νΘ and
ν0 . We proceed by induction on the scale ri , i ≥ 0. Assume we explored the sets of
interfaces Γ(ri ) and Γ0 (ri ) (interfaces up to radius ri ) according to some coupling of
νΘ and ν0 . These interfaces might be badly separated at radius ri . We sample their
continuation (independently under νΘ and ν0 ) until radius ri /2 thus obtaining using
the previous notations Γi and Γi0 (and the corresponding configurations of faces Θi and
Θi0 ). As we have seen, the event Wi that both configurations of faces are well-separated
is satisfied with positive probability.
     We now wish to sample the continuations Γ(ri+1 ) and Γ0 (ri+1 ) of these interfaces
up to radius ri+1 according to what have been explored so far, i.e., according to the
laws ν i and ν0i . If Wi does not hold, then the coupling “fails” at this scale and we
sample Γ(ri+1 ) \ Γi and Γ0 (ri+1 ) \ Γi0 independently, according to ν i and ν0i . Else, if Wi
holds, then by (3.3) and (3.4), with positive probability for both ν i and ν0i , the sets of
all interfaces crossing from ri+1 to 2ri+1 satisfy Ri . Furthermore, by (3.1) and (3.2),
any set of interfaces satisfying Ri has about the same probability under ν i or ν0i . This
allows us to sample Γ(ri+1 ) under ν i and Γ0 (ri+1 ) under ν0i and to couple these samples
so that the conditional probability of the event Si := {Υi = Υi0 ∈ Ri } is greater than
some absolute constant c > 0. Notice here that some care is needed since it is not Υi
that we are sampling according to ν i , but rather Γ(ri+1 ) \ Γi ; indeed Υi could consist
of more than 4 interfaces, but as we have seen, with positive probability there are only
4 of them, and in that case we have Υi ⊂ Γ(ri+1 ). It is easy to check that, if Si holds,
then the interfaces Γ(ri+1 ) and Γ0 (ri+1 ) induce exactly the same configuration of faces
Θ(ri+1 ) = Θ0 (ri+1 ) at radius ri+1 .
     The induction stops when Si has occurred or when i reaches N , whichever happens
first. Let i∗ ≤ N denote the index where the induction stopped. Call S the event that
the induction stopped at i∗ < N , i.e., the event that the coupling succeeded. If i∗ < N ,
then the configurations of faces at radius ri∗ +1 are identical for both partially discovered
configurations under the coupled νΘ and ν0 . Let us call this configuration of faces Θ∗ .
In both configurations, what remains to be sampled in DΘ∗ depends only on the faces
Θ∗ , and since we assumed τ = 1, they follow exactly the same law. Therefore, we can
sample identically for νΘ and ν0 and conditioned on Θ∗ the 4 interfaces which start at
the 4 endpoints of Θ∗ until they reach radius r. These interfaces, plus the faces Θ∗ if
needed, define the same faces around r for the coupled νΘ and ν0 , as desired.
     Let ν̂ denote the law of the coupling (νΘ , ν0 ) we have just constructed.
     It should be clear from what precedes that there is some universal constant c > 0
such that, at each scale 0 ≤ i < N , the coupling succeeds at scale ri with probability

                                              36
at least c. Indeed, knowing the interfaces Γ(ri ), Γ0 (ri ), up to radius ri , one has posi-
tive probability to obtain well separated interfaces Γi , Γi0 at radius ri /2; then if these
interfaces are indeed well separated, one couples the conditional measures ν i and ν0i
in such a way that the induced faces Θ(ri+1 ) and Θ0 (ri+1 ) are identical with positive
probability. This implies that for any 0 ≤ M ≤ N , the probability under the so-defined
coupling ν̂ that i∗ ≥ M is bounded above by (1 − C)M . Since N = blog8 (R/r)c, there
is indeed some absolute exponent k > 0 such that
                            ν̂ i∗ < N = ν̂ S > 1 − (r/R)k ,
                                         

which proves Proposition 3.1 in the case τ = 1.
    It remains to prove the case where τ = 0. The proof follows the exact same lines
as in the case τ = 1, plus the following color switching argument (we keep the same
notations). In the construction of the coupling ν̂, suppose we are at scale i < N and
that we already sampled Γi and Γi0 . If Wi holds, this allows us to sample Γ(ri+1 ) \ Γi
under ν i and Γ0 (ri+1 )\Γi+1
                          0   under ν0i and to couple these samples so that the conditional
probability of the event S̃i := {¬Υi = Υi0 ∈ Ri } is greater than some absolute constant
c > 0, where ¬Υ is the color-switched of Υ. With the same proof, the coupling succeeds
with probability at least 1 − (r/R)k , and in that case one ends up with two identical
faces Θ(r) and Θ0 (r) with reversed colors.
Remark 3.5. The proof adapts easily to the case of bond percolation on Z2 . The only
detail to handle is the color switching argument, since the duality on Z2 is not between
open and closed hexagons in the same lattice, but open edges and closed dual edges
(and vice versa). Since the dual of a percolation configuration in an r × (r + 1) box
lives in the (r + 1) × r dual box, it is better to take annuli A(r, R) = B(R) \ B(r),
where B(r) is an r × (r + 1) box. In Proposition 3.1, we have the measure νΘ with
τ = 0, and want to couple it with ν0 that has τ = 1. When we do the color switching
on νΘ , we get an annulus between (R + 1) × R and (r + 1) × r with the types of the
faces switched and the conditioning changed to τ = 1. But now this is just a 90 degrees
rotated version of a standard νΘ measure with the τ = 1 condition, hence we can do
our standard coupling, and the issue is solved.
   We will also need the following proposition, whose statement and proof are very
similar to those of Proposition 3.1.
Proposition 3.6. Let Ω be some piecewise smooth simply connected domain with 0 ∈ Ω.
Let d > 0 be the distance from 0 to the boundary ∂Ω and d0 = d ∧ 1. For any 0 < r < d0 ,
let A(r, ∂Ω) be the event that there are four alternating arms from the square of radius r
to the boundary ∂Ω. Also, let A(r, 1) be the event that there are four arms from radius
                                         d0
r to radius 1. For any 10η < r < 10         , let ν be the law on percolation configurations
conditioned on the event A(r, ∂Ω), and let ν0 be the law conditioned on the event A(r, 1).
    Then, there is a coupling of the conditional laws ν and ν0 such that with (conditional)
probability at least 1 − (r/d0 )k , the event G(r, d0 /2) (as defined previously) is satisfied

                                             37
for both configurations and the induced faces at radius r are identical. Here k > 0 is
some absolute exponent.

Sketch of proof. There is a small issue here compared to Proposition 3.1 which is that
there is no initial configuration of faces to start with. In particular, if one explores the
percolation configuration from ∂Ω towards some radius γ, there might be more than four
faces around
           √ γ. A way to deal with this minor issue is to choose an intermediate scale
γ (say, := r) and then argue (using quasi-multiplicativity) that with high conditional
probability (under A(r, ∂Ω)), there are only four arms from γ to ∂Ω. In more detail,
using A4 (·, ·) for the event of having at least four arms of alternating colors, and A5 (·, ·)
for the event that there are at least five arms, with four of them of alternating colors,
we have
                                                                                 
                                                       P A5 (γ, ∂Ω), A4 (r, ∂Ω)
        P A4 (γ, ∂Ω) \ A5 (γ, ∂Ω) A4 (r, ∂Ω) ≥ 1 −                         
                                                               P A4 (r, ∂Ω)
                                                                                
                                                         P A4 (r, γ) P A5 (γ, ∂Ω)
                                                  ≥1−                      
                                                               P A4 (r, ∂Ω)
                                                                       
                                                          P A5 (γ, ∂Ω)
                                                  ≥1−C                  = 1 − o(1) ,
                                                          P A4 (γ, ∂Ω)

where the last step (comparing the 4- and 5-arm probabilities) is a typical application
of the BK (van den Berg-Kesten) inequality, see [Gri99].
    On this large probability event, we have only four faces at radius γ, and can run
the proof of Proposition 3.1 from γ to r.

    The same proofs work for the 2-arm case, just using two faces instead of four. The
1-arm case is different, since one arm does not produce faces that separate the inside
from the outside. Instead, one may use open circuits there, and the proof is actually
simpler, since, due to monotonicity, one can use just FKG, no separation of interfaces
is needed. See Section 5 for more detail on these other cases.




                                              38
4     A measure on the set of pivotal points which is
      measurable with respect to the scaling limit




4.1    General setup and statement of convergence
In this section we define a natural scaling limit of the counting measure on pivotals,
normalized so that the set of points in a nice bounded domain (say, [0, 1]2 ) that are
1-important (i.e., have the alternating 4-arm event to distance at least 1, as in Sub-
section 1.3), or which are pivotal for a nice quad comparable to that domain (say, the
same [0, 1]2 ), have expected measure of order 1.
    Of course, on the discrete level, for a given configuration ωη , any point is pivotal
(or important) on some scale; for example, if the point happens to be surrounded by
at least 5 hexagons of the same color, this is scale is only η. So, in order to keep a
meaningful measure at the limit, we will only keep track of points in the mesh which
are pivotals on a macroscopic scale.
    This is consistent with our ultimate goal of proving that dynamical percolation,
as well as near-critical percolation, correctly rescaled, has a scaling limit. Indeed, as
we outlined in Subsection 1.1, if one is interested in the trajectory t 7→ ωtη up to
a certain small precision, it is enough to know the initial configuration ω0η , as well as
what happened on the set of points which were initially at least ρ-important (the choice
of ρ depends on the amount of precision that one requires).
    This step is made rigorous in [GPS13a]. In the current paper, we focus on the
scaling limit of the following (random) counting measures in the plane, parametrized
by the scale “cut-off” ρ > 0:
                                                    X                    η2
                         µ̄ρη = µ̄ρη (ωη ) :=                    δx              .   (4.1)
                                                x: ρ-important
                                                                      α4η (η, 1)

    Roughly speaking, ρ-important points are the same as points that are pivotal for

                                                  39
some “ρ-macroscopic” quad with boundary “not too close” to the point. For conve-
nience, we will actually consider measures which are defined in a somewhat less sym-
metric way, but will turn out to be less sensitive to local effects in our proof. This needs
some definitions:
Definition 4.1. Let A be some closed topological annulus of the plane; the bounded
component of Ac will be called its inside face; ∂1 A and ∂2 A will be its inner and outer
boundaries. We will say that A is a proper annulus if its inner and outer boundaries
are piecewise smooth curves of finite length.
Definition 4.2. Let H be a family of proper annuli in the plane. It will be called an
enhanced tiling if the collection of the inner boundaries form a locally finite tiling of
the plane. The diameter of H will be

                                 diam H := sup {diam A}.
                                              A∈H

    Let A be some proper annulus of the plane with inside face ∆; a point x ∈ ∆ in the
triangular grid of mesh η is called A-important if there are four alternating arms in
ωη from x to the outer boundary ∂2 A of A. We define the measure
                                                X                     η2
                        µA     A

probability that there is some A-important hexagon x intersecting ∂1 A is going to zero.
    We will now prove that for any fixed proper annulus A, the random measure µA  η (ωη )

has a scaling limit µ when η goes to zero, and moreover µ = µ (ω) is a measurable
function of the continuum percolation ω, as defined in Section 2.2. More precisely, we
have the following theorem:

Theorem 4.3. Let A be a fixed proper annulus of the plane. When η → 0, the random
variable (ωη , µA                                 A

percolation, and the measure µ = µ (ω) is a measurable function of ω.

4.2    Tightness and moment bounds
Firstly, we show that the family of variables {(ωη , µA   η )}η>0 is tight. In Section 2.2, we
defined ωη as a Borel measure on the compact separable metrizable space (HD , TD ),
hence {ωη }η>0 is obviously tight. It is a standard fact that if {Xη }η>0 , {Yη }η>0 are tight
families of variables, then, in any coupling, the coupled family of variables {(Xη , Yη )}η>0
is tight, as well. So, it is enough to prove that the family of measures {µA    η }η>0 is tight.
Since µA η are finite measures   supported   on  the  inside  face ∆,  proving tightness   boils
down to proving
                                  lim sup E µA
                                                    
                                               η (∆) < ∞ .
                                      η→0

This is straightforward by the definition of µAη . Indeed, let d > 0 be the distance
between ∂1 A and ∂2 A; a point in ∆ has to be d-important in order to be A-important.
Therefore, if d0 = d ∧ 1/2:
                              X 
                    E µA           P x is A-important η 2 α4η (η, 1)−1
                                                     

                                    x∈∆

                                    x∈∆

The approximate equality in the last line follows from quasi-multiplicativity, from the
fact that α4η (d0 , 1) depends on η but converges to the macroscopic probability α4 (d0 , 1)
when η goes to zero, and from the observation that

                                 lim ∆ ∩ ηT η 2 = area(∆) .
                                η→0



                                                  41
This observation can be proved by noticing that the area of points in ∆ with distance
at least η from ∂1 A converges to area(∆) as η → 0, giving asymptotically η −2 area(∆)
lattice points in ∆ ∩ ηT, while the number of lattice points at distance at most η from
∂1 A is at most O(η −1 length(∂1 A)).
    This proves tightness of {(ωη , µAη )}η>0 . Therefore, there exists some subsequential
                    A
scaling limit (ω, µ ) along some subsequence {ηk }k>0 , where ηk goes to 0. We will show
that this µA can actually be recovered from ω, which is the unique subsequential scaling
limit of {ωη }η>0 , as we already know from Section 2.2. Consequently, the pair (ω, µA )
will also be unique.

4.3    Strategy for the proof of uniqueness
Since the subsequential scaling limit µA is a measure, we will not need to check sigma-
additivity etc., we will only need to characterize uniquely the law of this random mea-
sure. For this, it will be enough to determine, for any ball B ⊂ ∆, the value of µA (B)
as a function of ω. The strategy of the proof is as follows. If η is a small mesh, we
are interested in µAη (B), that is, in the number X = Xη of points inside B which are


                                                          43
                                                       X
A-important (indeed, by definition, µA  η (B) := η −2 αη4 (η,1) ). We first need to show that X
can be “guessed” with arbitrarily good precision when one relies only on “macroscopic”
information, since only the macroscopic information is preserved in the scaling limit ω.
Then we will also have to prove the actual convergence of the measures µA             η . For the
approximation from macroscopic data, fix any grid of squares of radius  (i.e., of side-
length 2), and let Y = Yη be the number of squares Q in this grid which are contained
in B and which satisfy a 4-arm event from 2Q to ∂2 A. Why are we choosing 2Q instead
of simply Q? This will save us from some boundary issues in our later conditionings.
    One would like to show that, knowing Y = Yη , one can guess with good precision
what X = Xη is. In other words, for some well-chosen factor of proportionality β =
β(, η), one should have X ≈ β Y in some sense. We will see that there            is a natural
                                                                                             
candidate for this β-factor, and will show that for this β, one has E |X − βY |2 =
     2           2
o(E X ) = o(E βY ). It will be convenient to think of this property as a kind of law
of large numbers, even though we will in fact only achieve the above L2 -control (which
fortunately will be sufficient for our ultimate goal).
    Before going any further, let us make the above setup more precise. First of all,
let us fix the grid of -squares to be the grid G = G (a, θ) of the -squares centered
at the points of the lattice 2 eiθ Z2 + a, with θ ∈ R and a ∈ C. Why should one
consider all possible orientations of the -grid? In Section 6, we will show that the
asymptotic measure we are constructing satisfies some conformal covariance properties
(in particular, rotational invariance). With this perspective in mind, we should not
restrict ourselves to a macroscopic lattice of -squares conveniently chosen with respect
to the orientation of our triangular grid ηT. This is the reason for this additional
technicality.
    The following proposition will be the main step in the proof of the uniqueness of
the limiting measure.
Proposition 4.6. Let A be some proper annulus, and let B ⊂ ∆ be a ball included in
the inside face of A. Consider an -grid G corresponding to the lattice 2 eiθ Z2 + a, with
θ ∈ R and a ∈ C.
    Recall that X = X(ωη ) denotes the number of sites in ηT∩B which are A-important
and Y = Y  (ωη ) is the number of -squares Q in G ∩ B which satisfy the four-arm event
from 2Q to ∂2 A.
    Then, there is a deterministic quantity β = β(η, , a, θ) which satisfies
                                                        2
                            E (X − βY )2 ≤ ξ(η, ) E X ,
                                          
                                                                                      (4.8)

where ξ(η, ) goes to zero when  and η/ go to zero. Notice that the control we achieve is
independent of the orientation a, θ of the grid (which will be relevant later) but depends
on B ⊂ ∆ and A.
     Let us sketch the proof of this second moment estimate. Let Q1 , . . . , Qp denote the
list of -squares in the grid G which are contained in B. For each 1 ≤ i ≤ p, define yi to

                                               44
be the indicator function of the event that there are 4 arms from 2Qi to ∂2 A; define also
xi to be the number of A-important points inside Qi . Then one has X := x1 + . . . + xp
and Y = y1 + . . . + yp . Formally, we neglectedS here some boundary issues, since one
should also consider the points lying in B \ Qi . We will come back to this minor
                                                                            2
                                                                                       2
issue in the actual proof. We wish to obtain the estimate    E  |X  −

then analyze the first moment E X − βY . It can be rewritten as
                                  X             

                                       i

since yi = 0 implies xi = 0. Now, for any i, E xi yi = 1 is the expected number of A-
important points inside Qi knowing that there are already four arms from 2Qi to ∂2 A.
The coupling result Proposition 3.6 essentially says that this quantity should depend
very little on the shape of ∂2 A and on the position of Qi with respect to
                                                                         ∂2 A. In other
                                                                                   
words, by the coupling argument, we get that all these quantities E xi yi = 1 are
almost the same, and this common “agreement” is precisely what β should represent.
                                                                              
One could choose for β precisely one of these quantities (say, E x1 y1 = 1 ), but it
will be convenient to define β in a more universal way: i.e., based on some “reference”
square Q0 and some universal quad independent of ∂2 A (in the spirit of Proposition 3.1).
The details are postponed to the actual proof.
    We sketched this first moment analysis only to highlight where the β factor might
come from. What we really need is the second moment. It can be written as
                          X 
            E (X − βY )2 =
                                                      
                                 E xi − βyi xj − βyj
                              i,j
                             X                                 
                           =  E yi yj E xi − β xj − β yi = 1, yj = 1 .                 (4.9)
                              i,j

    In this sum over squares Qi , Qj , there are relatively few pairs of nearby squares (say,
whose distance d(Qi , Qj ) is less than r, with   r  1). Hence one can neglect these
pairs of squares, or in other words, we can neglect the near-diagonal term in (4.9) for
a well-chosen scale r. Now, for any two squares Qi , Qj such that d(Qi , Qj ) ≥ r  ,
if one conditions on {yi = 1, yj = 1}, i.e., on the event that both 2Qi and 2Qj are
A-important, then, again by the coupling argument, one expects that the configuration
seen inside Qi should be
                         almost independent
                                                of
                                                  what is seen inside
                                                                   Qj . This should
                                                                                     lead
to E xi − β xj − β yi = 1, yj = 1 ≈ E xi − β yi = 1 E xj − β yj = 1 . Now,
since β is precisely chosen to match well with these first moment quantities, one should
indeed obtain a small second moment in (4.9).
    However, in order to apply the coupling results from Section 3, there are some issues
about the above conditioning. Conditioned on the entire configuration outside Qi and

                                             45
Qj in a way that makes {yi = yj = 1} possible, the value of xj and yj might not at
all be independent of the configuration inside Qi . See Figure 4.1. This shows that
somehow the configurations inside Qi and Qj interfere with each other in a nontrivial
way, which is bad news for applying our coupling results from Section 3.



                   Qi


                     Qj

                  ∂1 A
                           ∂2 A

Figure 4.1: Assume that all disjoint arms are shown between Qi , Qj and ∂2 A. Then,
in the first example, xj > 0 requires a blue (dashed) connection within Qi , while, in
the second one, it requires a red (solid) connection. In the third example, xi and xj are
independent.

    To handle this interference, first take some enlarged square Q0i around Qi so that
Qj ⊂ (Q0i )c . Under the conditioning {yi = yj = 1}, one can further condition on
all the percolation configuration seen in (Q0i )c (and thus, in particular, we know all the
information inside Qj ). The hope is that if Q0i is much larger than Qi , then the coupling
results will imply that the configuration inside Qi is basically independent of everything
we have conditioned on, except that we still have the same interference as before: even
though we know all the information inside Qj , the set of A-important points in Qj
might still depend on how things are connected inside Q0i . If the configuration around
Q0i has many faces (with the definition of Section 3), then this connectivity information
could be quite complicated, hence it would be very convenient to assume that there
is a configuration Θ of only four faces around Q0i (four being the minimum number
compatible with the condition {yi = 1}). Then the only information inside Q0i which
remains relevant outside Q0i is whether the open arcs of Θ are connected or not inside
Q0i (or rather DΘ ). This missing internal information is given by the random variable
UΘ introduced in Section 3. If F denotes the filtration generated by the sites in (Q0i )c
                 c
(or rather in DΘ   ), summarizing the above discussion, we obtain that once conditioned
on F and on the variable UΘ , the number xj of A-important points inside Qj is known.
Hence one can write
                                                                        
              E (xi − βyi )(xj − βyj ) = E (xj − βyj )E xi − βyi F, UΘ ,
                                                     
which allows us, by focusing on E xi − βyi F, UΘ , to “decouple” the behavior inside
the Qi box from what is outside Q0i . Note that this strategy explains why our main
coupling result in Section 3 dealt with this additional conditioning on UΘ .

                                            46
     But we still need to justify why one can assume that there are indeed 4 faces around
Q0i . This is obviously not necessarily the case, especially if Q0i is of size comparable to
d(Qi , Qj ) ≥ r. To make sure that with high conditional probability (under {yi = 1}),
there are only four faces around Q0i , a solution is to fix the radius of our enlarged box
Q0i at some intermediate scale γ so that   γ  r  1. Indeed, now it is unlikely
(under {yi = 1}) that there will be 5 arms connecting Q0i and Qj (the five-arm event
being much less likely than the four-arm event).
   The actual proof in the coming subsection will be rather technical: we will need to
handle these various intermediate scales   γ  r  1 as well as some issues coming
from the discrete lattice. We will encounter some additional technicalities during the
proof that we chose to hide in the above outline. Nevertheless, this sketch of proof
should serve as a reading-guide for the next subsection.

Let qi and qj be the respective centers of these squares. Let γ ∈ (2, r/4) be some inter-

Q(Υ) will denote the least distance between the endpoints of the interfaces on ∂B(qi , γ)
normalized by γ. Let A4 = A4 (γ, l/2) be the event that there are at least four arms of
alternating colors in the annulus B(qi , l/2) \ B(qi , γ). Furthermore, let A5 be the event
that there are at least five arms in the same annulus, with four of them of alternating
colors. Recall that G = G(γ, l/2) is the event that there are exactly four alternating
arms (thus G = A4 \ A5 ), and T α = T α (γ, l/2) is the event that {Q(Υ) > α}, with the
quality cut-off α to be fixed later. We now define the following disjoint events:
                               

                                  Zi = A5 ∪ (A4 ∩ ¬T α ) .

4.5    Ratio limit theorems
In this subsection, we state and prove some limit theorems that will be used in the
sequel and are also interesting in their own right. Their relevance to the existence and
conformal covariance of the limit of the measures µAη will be explained at the beginning
of Subsection 4.6.
    Aa,θ
      (r, R) will denote the four-arm event from the rotated square B(a, r) = a +
e [−r, r)2 to the rotated square ∂B(a, R) with the additional requirement that open
 iθ

arms are connected to the (rotated) right-left boundaries and closed arms are connected
                                                                               η,a,θ
to the upper-lower boundaries. The probability of this event is denoted by α        (r, R).
     a,θ            η,a,θ
By A (η, R) and α (η, R), we mean the four-arm event from the hexagon containing
a. Events and probabilities with the subscript 4 always refer to the standard four-arm
events between the standard unrotated squares. Finally, omitting the superscript η
from an α-probability means it is understood in the scaling limit.

Proposition 4.9. For any fixed r > 0,

                                α4η (η, r)       α4 (, r)
                            lim η          = lim           = r−5/4 .                    (4.28)
                            η→0 α4 (η, 1)    →0 α4 (, 1)


Furthermore, there is an absolute constant C > 0, such that, uniformly in the shift and
orientation, a, eiθ ,
                             αη,a,θ (η, 1)      αa,θ (, 1)
                         lim  η           = lim           =C.                  (4.29)
                         η→0 α4 (η, 1)       →0 α4 (, 1)

Remark 4.10. This proposition might appear obvious at the first sight, and highly non-
trivial at the second, but the truth is in between. The issue is that although we know
the critical exponent 5/4, the probability α4η (η, 1) is only known to be η 5/4+o(1) , so there
could be large but sub-polynomial factors, while the scaling limit quantity α4 (, 1) is
known to be 5/4 only up to constant factors. Therefore, the proposition is not a direct
consequence of the determination of the exponent, and, to our knowledge, is a new
result in itself. On the other hand, we do not have to improve the exponent results to
prove our results: somehow, the possible sub-polynomial corrections cancel out in the
quotients under interest.

    One would like at this stage to conclude that almost surely, µ? (B) = µA (B)(ω); this

indicator functions of balls do not behave well with respect to the weak* topology,

Remark 4.14 below regarding the issues that might appear.) It is a standard technique
to use Riemann sums for such an extension, and we get the following proposition:

Remark 4.14. Proposition 4.13 is actually weaker than the convergence of the measures
for a countable basis of balls Bj ⊂ ∆, j ≥ 1. If, for example, µ? happened to have

                                              64
Dirac point masses, then the convergence of integrals of continuous functions might not
imply the convergence of the measures of balls, hence one would need some additional
regularity property for the possible weak limits µ? . This also means that the weak*-
convergence to µ∗ does not alone imply the convergence for balls, i.e., the L2 -limit
µA (B)(ω) might not be equal to µ∗ (B) a.s. For any given ball B, one could easily prove
equality (see Corollary 4.16 below), but for all balls B simultaneously the situation is
more involved, so we chose not to address this question.
Remark 4.15. In (4.39) and (4.42), we have convergence only in L2 , not almost surely.
We expect that the stronger versions also hold, but our strategy does not seem to yield
this, or at least not without a lot of additional work. For comparison, one might consider
the convergence of the random Riemann-Stieltjes sums to the Itô integral. This holds
only in L2 in general, not almost surely; however, it is not very hard to see that for
reasonably regular functions (say, Hölder() for some  > 0) that do not depend on the
Brownian motion we are integrating against, the convergence does hold a.s.

Proof of Theorem 1.1. The proof is basically the same as for Theorem 4.3, with the
following modifications. We define the variables xi , yi , X, Y using not A-importance,
but Q-pivotality. The definition of β does not have to be changed. The measurability
of Y in the scaling limit of percolation now relies on Remark 2.11. For the application
of the coupling arguments to the L2 -approximation, there is the following issue: for
those Qi boxes in the -grid that are close to ∂Q, the enlarged γ-box Q0i does not lie
in Q, hence there is no room to apply the coupling lemma. The solution is to notice
that there are actually no Q-pivotals close to ∂Q, so, for small enough , we can ignore

                                              65
the -boxes close to ∂Q. What do we mean by “no pivotals close to ∂Q”? If an -box
Qi is such that the γ-box Q0i intersects ∂Q, then Qi can contain pivotals only if Q0i
has the 3-arm event to the remaining three boundary arcs of ∂Q. (Or, if Q0i intersects
two boundary arcs, then it needs to satisfy a 2-arm event.) But the boundary of ∂Q is
assumed to be piecewise smooth, the half-plane 3-arm exponent is 2, and the number of
possible essentially different such γ-boxes is O(1/γ), hence, by Markov’s inequality, the
probability that there exists such a γ-box goes to 0 as γ → 0, uniformly in η. Therefore,
in the joint coupling of ωη and ω, there is a random positive distance between ∂Q and
the closest pivotal, and the coupling lemma can be applied. These estimates also show
that the measures µQ  η are still tight, despite the presence of the boundary. Hence all
the arguments work fine.


4.7    Filtering
It was convenient to introduce the measures µAη for some proper annulus A ⊂ C instead
of working directly with µ̄ρη , the counting measure on ρ-important points. Indeed,
suppose that in the previous proof we were working with ρ-important points instead
of A-important points. Then, for different points x, y inside some -square Qi , given
some configuration of faces around Qi , we might need quite different information about
where these faces are connected outside Qi if we want to know how x and how y has
to be connected to these faces from the inside in order to be ρ-important. Say, if one
of the four arms emanating from the faces around Qi goes to distance ρ −  but not to
ρ, then it might happen that some points in Qi that are connected “pivotally” to the
four arms will be ρ-important while others will not. A-important points are simpler to
handle in this respect.
    If one wants to use the more natural concept of ρ-important points, then needs to
relate in some way the measures µA                       ρ
                                     η to the measures µ̄η . The following partial order
between enhanced tilings will handle this issue.
Definition 4.17. Let us say that an enhanced tiling H refines another, H0 , denoted
by H ≤ H0 , if the following holds: for any pair of annuli A = B2 \ B1 ∈ H and
A0 = B20 \ B10 ∈ H0 , if the inner faces B1 and B10 intersect each other, then B2 ⊂ B20 .
   For example, one can consider the enhanced tiling

                     Hηρ := B(x, ρ) \ {x} : all η-tiles x of D
                           


in a domain D. Now, if H is an enhanced tiling with diam H < ρ, then H ≤ Hηρ . On
the other hand, if d(∂1 A, ∂2 A) > ρ for all A ∈ H, then H ≥ Hηρ .
    The point of this definition is that if H ≤ H0 , then we have the reversed domination
                                                                H0
between the associated annulus-pivotal measures: µH      η ≥ µη . Therefore, there is a
coupled pair (P, P 0 ) of Poisson samples from these measures such that P ⊃ P 0 . In
particular, if H() :  ∈ I is an ordered family of enhanced tilings, i.e., H(δ) ≤ H()


                                           66
                                                                        H()
whenever δ < , for δ,  ∈ I ⊂ R+ , then for each η > 0 we get a family µη :  ∈ I
of increasing measures (as  decreases), called a filtered measure, and there is an

          increasing family of Poisson samples P(H()) :  ∈ I .
    If H() :  ∈ I is an ordered family of enhanced tilings satisfying diam H() < 
and d(∂1 A, ∂2 A) > /2 for all A ∈ H(), then we have the following dominations

                                                ρ

This is a useful tool for comparing annulus-pivotality to ρ-pivotality.


5     Limit results for other special points
We will now explain how to extend the above techniques to the case of counting measures
on other geometrical objects of interest in critical percolation, namely:

    • An “area”-measure on the clusters.

    • A “length”-measure for interfaces (SLE6 curves in the scaling limit).

    • A “length”-measure on exterior boundaries (SLE8/3 curves).

These three families of measures will be called cluster measures, interface measures and
frontier measures, respectively.
   One difference from the case of the pivotal measure is that the σ-algebra in which the
limit measures will be measurable will not always be the Borel σ-algebra of the quad-
crossing space, but, for instance, the interface measure will be defined as a function of
the SLE6 curve.
    The proofs are in large part very similar to the proof given for the pivotal measure,
hence we will only highlight the places that need modifications. The first case is much
easier to establish due to the monotonicity of the one-arm event. The second one is
very similar to the construction of the pivotal measure (except that four-arm events are
replaced by two-arm events), while we will see that the third one requires some more
care. In general, the analog of Section 4 carries through easily in each case, while the
coupling part (Section 3) needs some fixing that depends on the number of arms.
   Finally, after the construction of the cluster measure, we will prove a corollary of
independent interest on the so-called two-point function in percolation, namely that
the two-point connectivity function is asymptotically rotationally invariant.




                                           67
5.1    The cluster measure (or area measure)




   In this subsection, we wish to construct an “area”-measure on the clusters of critical
percolation. Similarly to the rest of the paper, a natural way to proceed is to consider
the properly rescaled counting measures on “macroscopic” clusters. Let ρ > 0 be some
cut-off length and consider the following rescaled measure on the clusters of an ωη
percolation configuration in ηT whose diameters are greater than ρ:
                                                X                       1
                       λρη = λρη (ωη ) :=                    δx                   ,   (5.1)
                                                                  η −2 α1η (η, 1)
                                            x: diam(Cx )>ρ


where for each x ∈ ηT, Cx denotes the cluster attached to x.
   For the same reasons that we encountered in the case of pivotals, it turns out to be
more convenient to work with the following related measures: for any proper annulus
A, define
                                         X              1
                      λA     A
                       η = λη (ωη ) :=          δx −2 η        .                  (5.2)
                                                   η α1 (η, 1)
                                             x: {x↔∂2 A}

   With techniques similar to the ones used for the pivotal measure, one can prove
the following analog of Theorem 4.3. We will only explain below what adaptations are
needed.

Theorem 5.1. Let A be a fixed proper annulus of the plane. When η → 0, the ran-
dom variable (ωη , λA                                  A
                     η ) converges in law to some (ω, λ ), where ω is the scaling limit of
                                         A     A
critical percolation, and the measure λ = λ (ω) is a measurable function of ω. The
measure thus defined may be thought of as an area measure on macroscopic clusters
of percolation.

    A filtering argument as in Subsection 4.7 allows us, if needed, to deal with the initial
{λρ }ρ>0 measures.


                                                 68
    Rough sketch of proof. Due to the monotonicity of the one-arm event, the proof
is in many ways much simpler than the one for the pivotal measure. The reason for
this is that all the separation of arms type of results needed in Sections 3 and 4 are not
needed here. RSW is the only necessary tool in this case.
    Let us first sketch what the analog of the coupling part (Section 3) is. We start
with some notations. If η < r < R, let A1 (r, R) be the one-arm event from radius
r to radius R. If Ω is any smooth simply connected domain and η < r is such that
B(0, r) ∩ ∂Ω = ∅, define A1 (r, ∂Ω) to be the event that there is an open path from
∂B(0, r) to ∂Ω. Note that, in this definition, B(0, r) need not be included in Ω. Also
if Ω = B(0, R), this event coincides with A1 (r, R), so we will only state the coupling
result in this general setup.
    Now if η < r < u, let Γ = Γ(r, u) be the outermost open circuit in the annulus
A(r, u), i.e., the simple open circuit which is the closest to ∂B(0, u). If there are no
such circuits, then let Γ := ∅. It is a standard fact that such a circuit can be revealed
in a “Markovian” way, only using bits from the exterior of Γ in such a way that the
region surrounded by Γ is left untouched.
    The analog of the coupling result that we need is the following:

Proposition 5.2. Let Ω be some piecewise smooth simply connected domain with 0 ∈
Ω \ ∂Ω. Let d > 0 be the distance from 0 to the boundary ∂Ω and d0 = d ∧ 1.
                          d0
    For any 10η < r < 100    , let ν be the law on percolation configurations conditioned on
the event A1 (r, ∂Ω), and let ν0 be the law conditioned on the event A1 (r, 1).
                       0
    Let h := blog2 ( dr )c and u := 2h/2 r. Let Γ = Γ(r, u) and Γ0 = Γ0 (r, u) be the
outermost contours under ν and ν 0 .
    Then, there is a coupling of the conditional laws ν and ν 0 such that with (conditional)
probability at least 1 − (r/d0 )k , both Γ and Γ0 are non-empty and are identical, where
k > 0 is some absolute exponent.

    The proof of this coupling is essentially in Kesten’s work on the IIC [Kes86], but
let us briefly explain how to adapt the strategy of Section 3 to this case. Namely, one
tries to couple the two measures in each dyadic annulus ranging from d0 to u = 2h/2 r,
where “dyadic” will actually correspond to log8 , for convenience. Roughly speaking, in
each of these annuli, say A(s, 8s), with positive probability there are circuits in each
of A(2s, 4s), A(4s, 6s) and A(6s, 8s). Let Γ1 , Γ2 , Γ3 be respectively the outermost
circuit in A(2s, 4s), the innermost one in A(4s, 6s), and the outermost one in A(6s, 8s).
Following the notations of Section 3, let S = S(ωη ) be the union of all hexagons which
are determined by Γ1 and Γ2 plus all hexagons which lie between Γ1 and Γ2 . Let also
mS be the number of hexagons that are in S.
    Whenever there is an open circuit in A(6s, 8s), which happens with positive condi-
tional probability under A1 (r, 1) or A1 (r, ∂Ω), we can explore A(6s, 8s) from the outside
in a way that detects the outermost circuit Γ3 and does not touch anything inside Γ3 .
Then, using RSW, one easily obtains that there is some constant 0 < c < ∞ such that,


                                            69
for any admissible S,
                  2−mS /c ≤ P S(ωη ) = S ∃ Γ3 , A1 (r, Γ3 ) ≤ c2−mS .
                                                          

    Now, following the same technology as in Section 3, one has that with high probabil-
ity (1−(u/d0 )k1 for some k1 > 0), the coupling succeeds before reaching the intermediate
radius u = 2h/2 r, i.e., we have identical circuits Γ1 and Γ2 in the two configurations,
given by ν and ν 0 , respectively. Since the exploration was Markovian so far, one can
now couple these two measures so that they match inside Γ1 . Then, with high (con-
ditional) probability 1 − (r/u)k2 , there is an (outermost) open circuit Γ = Γ(r, u) in
A(r, u). By construction, this contour is identical for the two measures and can be
discovered in a Markovian way from the outside (so, this contour could be thought of
as a “stopping time”).
    Now, as with the pivotal points, it remains to use this coupling property in order
to prove Theorem 5.1. It is straightforward to adapt Section 4 to our present case.
Again, the present situation is much simpler in many ways. For example, if one defines
X and Y as before, then, in the second moment estimate, two -squares Qi and Qj in
general interact very little (while, with the pivotal points, this interaction was a non-
negligible issue). The reason for this is that if one conditions Qi and Qj to be part of
a large cluster, then with high (conditional) probability, there are open circuits around
Qi and Qj disconnecting one from the other. This implies that with high conditional
probability the behavior in one box is decorrelated
                                                     from the behavior in the other one.
                     2                              2               2
    So, we get the L -approximation E (X − βY ) = o((EX) ), using

to ω (i.e., Y ,η → Y  = Y  (ω)). This is precisely the purpose of Lemma 2.9.


                                             70
5.2    Rotational invariance of the two-point function
The result of this subsection uses rotational invariance of the scaling limit plus the
coupling technology for one arm, Proposition 5.2. Since, as we mentioned in the previous
subsection, the coupling idea was already a key ingredient in [Kes86], this result is not
fundamentally new; however, we do not know of an explicit appearance of it so far, so
we decided to include it here to highlight the power of the coupling ideas.
   The asymptotic rotational invariance of the two-point function in critical percolation
on Zd for d ≥ 19 was proved by very different methods by Hara [Har08].

Proposition 5.3. There exists a universal constant C > 0 such that if x and y are two
sites of ηT, with Euclidean distance d = d(x, y) > 0 (hence graph distance ∼ g(θ) d/η,

as η → 0, uniformly in the angle θ.
