5.3    The interface measure (related to the natural parametriza-
       tion of SLE6 curves)




   Interfaces between open and closed clusters have been much studied since the dis-
covery of the SLE processes. When the mesh η goes to zero, these curves are known
to converge towards SLE6 curves. At the scaling limit, these curves are classically
parametrized by their “capacity”. This capacity parametrization also makes sense on

                                           73
the discrete level for the exploration processes γη at mesh η, but it is very different
from the natural parametrization on γη which consists in counting the number of iter-
ated steps done by the exploration process so far. Whence the question of defining a
parametrization of the SLE6 curve at the scaling limit, which would be, in an appro-
priate sense, the scaling limit of the natural discrete parametrizations.
   In this subsection, we prove a result in this direction. Let us define some notation
before stating the main result. Let (Ω, a, b) be a smooth domain with two marked
points on its boundary. For any mesh η > 0, let (Ωη , aη , bη ) be the discrete domain
approximating (Ω, a, b) (in any “reasonable” way, say from inside for example). Let γη
denote the chordal exploration process (with Dobrushin’s boundary conditions) from
aη to bη . By definition, γη consists of all edges e of the hexagonal lattice which lie
between an open hexagon connected to the open arc and a closed hexagon connected to
the closed arc. Each edge e corresponds to one iteration of the exploration path, hence
each edge contributes one unit of time to the natural parametrization. We thus define
the following counting measure supported on γη :
                                                      X                   η2
                      τη = τη (ωη ) = τη (γη ) :=                δe              .    (5.8)
                                                    edges e∈γη
                                                                      α2η (η, 1)

    As in the case of the pivotal measure or the cluster measure, we would like to show
that this counting measure τη , which we will call the interface measure, has a scaling
limit when η → 0. More precisely, we would like the joint (ωη , τη ) to converge towards a
coupling (ω, τ ), where τ = τ (ω) would be measurable with respect to the scaling limit.
    One could prove such a statement (following the setup of Sections 3 and 4), but this
would have the disadvantage that the exact relation of the resulting τ = τ (ω) to the
SLE6 curve γ (the scaling limit of the exploration paths γη ) would be unclear.
    To start with, even the measurability of γ w.r.t. ω is unresolved, see Question 2.14
at the end of Subsection 2.4. But, assuming an affirmative answer to that question,
γ contains much less information than ω. In definition (5.8) of the discrete interface
measure, we wrote τη = τη (ωη ) = τη (γη ): the amount of information in ωη and γη
relevant to τη is obviously the same. But it is not clear what happens in the scaling
limit. Hence, at least assuming Question 2.14, having a scaling limit measure τ =
τ (γ) measurable w.r.t. the SLE curve γ would be stronger and more satisfying than
measurability w.r.t. the entire quad-crossing configuration ω. Therefore, this is the
path we are taking.
   One more issue to mention is whether the interface measure τ can be considered
as a time parametrization of the SLE6 curve γ. We expect so, but as explained in
Subsection 1.2, the measure does not see the order of points in which the curve is
traversed, hence additional work is needed. Even if we assume that the support of τ is
the entire range of γ, which will be proved in [GP], we still have the following questions.
For any subdomain F that contains a neighbourhood of the starting point a, let γF ⊂ γ

                                             74
be the curve stopped upon first exiting F , and let τF be the measure collected so far.
Then we clearly have τF (γF ) ≤ τ (γF ), but do we have equality? If not, then we clearly
do not have a time parametrization by τ . Moreover, we need almost sure equality not
only for a fixed F , but for all F simultaneously. We will try to address these questions
in [GP].
    Now, let us briefly recall what the setup of convergence of γη towards SLE6 is. It
is a convergence in law under the Hausdorff topology on simple curves. See [Wer07]
for more detail on this. For simplicity, let us restrict ourselves to the case where the
domain Ω (with two marked points a, b ∈ ∂Ω) is smooth and bounded. We consider
our exploration processes γη as continuous paths γη : [0, 1] → Ω, such that γη (0) = a
and γη (1) = b. The space C of such curves γ (which lie in Ω) is equipped with the
(pseudo)-distance
                          d(γ, γ 0 ) = inf sup |γ(u) − γ 0 (φ(u))| ,
                                     φ u∈[0,1]

where the infimum is taken over all continuous increasing bijections of [0, 1] onto itself.
Let Tk·k∞ be the topology on C generated by this distance. The important theorem by
Smirnov [Smi01, Smi06] is that the discrete exploration paths γη converge in law, in
the sense of the Borel σ-field of (C , Tk·k∞ ), towards an SLE6 curve in Ω from a to b (see
also [CN07]).
    We wish to prove the following theorem (an analog of Theorem 1.1):

Theorem 5.5. Let Ω be a smooth bounded domain of the plane with two marked points
a, b ∈ ∂Ω. When η → 0, the random variable (γη , τη ) converges in law, under the
topology of (C , Tk·k∞ ), to (γ, τ ), where γ is a chordal SLE6 in Ω from a to b, and the
measure τ = τ (γ) is a measurable function of γ. We call this random measure the
length measure of γ.

Remark 5.6. The same theorem holds for non-bounded smooth domains (6= C), but for
simplicity we stick to this case (essentially this would boil down to looking at larger
and larger bounded regions in Ω).
Proof. As in Section 4, we first discuss tightness and boundary issues, then we char-
acterize uniquely the subsequential scaling limits.
Tightness and treating the boundary issues. As in Subsection 4.2, in order to
prove the tightness of the measures τη (as the mesh η goes to zero), one would have
to show that in expectation, the total mass τη (Ω) remains bounded as η → 0. In the
bulk, this is done very similarly to Subsection 4.2, but near the boundary, this would
already require some care. Still, even if we succeeded in showing this, it could still be
that at the scaling limit, a positive fraction of the measure would be concentrated on
the boundary ∂Ω. This is a scenario that we definitively want to exclude — otherwise,
the measure could look quite strange. Therefore, we need to prove that the measure
gets smaller near the boundary. More precisely, for any δ > 0, if Ω(δ) denotes the points


                                            75
in Ω at distance at least δ from the boundary, then we would like to show that

                                              τη (Ω \ Ω(δ) ) = o(1) ,

where o(1) goes to zero when δ → 0, uniformly in η < δ/10. Note that this implies
tightness in Ω, as well.
    The proof of this estimate, though not conceptually hard, needs some rather tedious
computations. We will here only highlight briefly how it works. (See [GPS10a] where
many such boundary issues were treated carefully.) Divide the set Ω \ Ω(δ) into  1/δ
squares of size δ. Roughly speaking (ignoring the effects of the possible curvature of
∂Ω), group these squares in a dyadic fashion depending on their distance from the set
{a, b}. This singles out the two squares which touch the tips a and b. Group further
all the sites in these two squares dyadically depending on their distance from a and
b, respectively. In all the other δ-boxes, group the sites dyadically according to their
distance from ∂Ω. In the δ-box at a, at distance about 2k η from a, the probability of
a site to be on γη is roughly α2η (η, 2k η), and there are roughly 22k such sites. So, their
contribution to the un-normalized expected length measure is
                             O(log(δ/η))
                                X
                                          α2η (η, 2k η) 22k  η −2 α2η (η, 1) δ 7/4+o(1) .
                                k=1


In the δ-boxes at unit order distance from a and b, for a site at distance about 2k η
from ∂Ω, the probability of being on γη is roughly α2η (η, 2k η) α1+,η (2k η, 1). In all these
δ-boxes, there are about 2k /η such sites. So, their total contribution to the expectation
is
              O(log(δ/η))
                 X
                           α2η (η, 2k η) α1+,η (2k η, 1) 2k /η  α2η (η, δ) α1+,η (δ, 1) δ/η 2
                 k=1

                                                                  η −2 α2η (η, 1) δ −1/4+1/3+1+o(1)
                                                                 = η −2 α2η (η, 1) δ 13/12+o(1) .

After normalization by η −2 α2η (η, 1), both contributions go to 0 with δ → 0. (For
instance, the rate δ 13/12 corresponds to fact that the 7/4-dimensional curve γ has a
2/3-dimensional intersection with the boundary, so in this 2/3-dimensional subset the
“7/4-dimensional measure” should scale with exponent 7/4 − 2/3 = 13/12.) The con-
tributions of the δ-boxes whose distance from {a, b} is less than order 1 but more than
zero is handled by a dyadic grouping again, and we are done.
Characterization of the subsequential scaling limits. Here, the whole setup
carries through easily. Let B be a ball inside Ω; we wish to approximate τη (B) using
macroscopic information. Let us then define Y = Yη to be the number of -squares Q
of B (in the same grid G as in Section 4, but let us not worry here about the orientation

                                                          76
of the grid) which are such that the square 2Q is connected via an open arm to the arc
ab and is connected via a closed arm to the opposite arc ba. Note that this is the same
as asking that γη ∩ 2Q 6= ∅. The number we wish to approximate is

                                                   X
                                  τη (B) =                   ,
                                             η −2 α4η (η, 1)

where X = Xη is the number of edges e ∈ ηT ∩ B which lie on the interface γη .
    It is straightforward to adapt the coupling argument (Section 3) to the case of the
two-arm event. Basically the only change is that one deals with configurations of two
faces, instead of four. Using this coupling result and following the details of Section 4,
one ends up with
                           E (X − βtwo−arm Y )2 = o(E X 2 ) ,
                                                       

where the proportionality factor βtwo−arm is the analog of β in Section 4.
    There is one part though which needs some more words of explanation: for the
pivotal measure, we used the fact that Yη converged to Y  = Y  (ω). This was a direct
consequence of Lemma 2.9. Since, we do not rely on the quad-crossing topology in this
subsection, we need an analog of Lemma 2.9 in our present setup. Namely, we need the
following result:

Proposition 5.7. If Q is any square included in (Ω, a, b), then
                                                         
                      P γη ∩ Q 6= ∅ −→ P SLE6 ∩ Q 6= ∅ .
                                         η→0


Moreover, in any coupling with γn → SLE6 a.s., we have the convergence in probability
of the indicator variables of the events in question.

    This “continuity result” about the convergence of discrete exploration paths towards
SLE6 is somewhat folklore in the community. A sketch of this proposition can be found
in [SW01]. The complete proof is not hard but a bit technical: the main idea is to use
the 3-arm event in H in order to justify that it is very unlikely for an interface γη or an
SLE6 to come close to ∂Q, without intersecting Q.




                                             77
5.4    Hints for the frontier measure and a natural parametrization
       of SLE8/3 curves




    Here we would want the normalized counting measure on the percolation fron-
tier, or exterior boundary of large clusters. Namely, we say that an open hexagon
neighbouring the interface γη is on the open frontier Ψ+ if it has not just one, but two
disjoint open arms to the open boundary arc. The closed frontier Ψ− is defined anal-
ogously. The right normalization for these points is clearly the polychromatic 3-arm
event:
                                                           X        η2
                ψη± = ψη± (ωη ) = ψη± (γη ) = ψη± (Ψ±
                                                    η ) :=    δ x η        .        (5.9)
                                                            ±
                                                                 α3 (η, 1)
                                                        x∈Ψ

    The scaling limit for this measure would need a bit more work than the other
cases. The issue is that three arms is much less appropriate for our setup of faces Θ in
Section 3: having two arms of the same colour next to each other means that the 3-arm
event is not characterized purely by interfaces that would produce faces and would cut
information between past (a percolation configuration outside a large box) and future
(the arrival of interfaces or arms at the small target box). The solution is to take a
mixture of the approaches in the 2-arm and 1-arm cases, and use two interfaces plus
RSW circuits to cut the information between the two interfaces on that side where
we need the two arms of the same colour. Another small issue is that the separation
of interfaces results of Appendix A cannot be used automatically: instead of an even
number of interfaces, we would need to work with three well-chosen arms.
    We do not go into the details, mainly because we do not have good applications in
mind. In what σ-algebra would one want to have the limit measure be measurable? The
quad-crossing configuration ω is one possibility, for which the 3-arm case of Lemma 2.9
can be used. This would be useful to measure the size of the exterior boundary of a
large percolation cluster, which is a reasonable but much less important goal than the
pivotal measure. On the other hand, measurability w.r.t. to the frontier itself (defined as


                                            78
a curve) would be less nice than the case of interface measure, because the frontier has a
scaling limit that is closely related to SLE8/3 , but is not that exactly. Getting a natural
parametrization of SLE8/3 by tweaking the frontier measure would certainly be much
less natural and exciting than getting it, say, from Self-Avoiding Walk paths. Finally,
measurability w.r.t. the interface scaling limit SLE6 could possibly be interesting from
some SLE duality point of view, but this again does not seem to be such a natural
choice.

      sures
We first discuss the annulus-important and quad-pivotal measures µA and µQ , then the
cluster and interface measures λA and τ Ω,a,b in Subsection 6.4.

Remark 6.2. Using the conformal invariance of the scaling limit, fromR the almost sure
equality in the theorem we get that µf (A) (f (B)) has the same law as B |f 0 |3/4 dµA .

   Since any conformal map is locally a rotation times a dilatation, we will, as a warm-
up, first check the theorem on these particular cases. This will be easier than the general
case, mainly because the grid of -squares that we used in defining the approximating
macroscopic quantities Y  is preserved quite nicely under rotations and dilatations,
while distorted by a general conformal map f .




                                                  79
6.1    Rotational invariance
Let us consider some proper annulus A of the plane, some ball B ⊂ ∆, and the rotation
T : z 7→ exp(iθ) z by an angle θ. We need to show that

                                µA (B, ω) = µT A (T B, T ω) .                            (6.1)

    By (4.39), the right hand side equals lim Y G(),T A (T B, T ω)/F (), an L2 -limit, where
G() is our usual grid of -squares and F () := −2 α4 (, 1)/c. Or, by using a rotated grid
for the approximation in (4.39), it is also equal to lim Y T G(),T A (T B, T ω)/F (), which
(by rotating back the entire universe) is trivially the same as lim Y G(),A (B, ω)/F (),
giving the left hand side of (6.1), as desired.
Remark 6.3. One might speculate that this type of rotational invariance should hold
even if we have a scaling limit ω without (or unproved) rotational invariance (such as
a subsequential limit of critical percolation on Z2 ), since the backbone of the above
argument seems to be the following: µA is a function of ω, and the definition of this
function in (4.39) does not depend on any special orientation θ, hence if one rotates ω,
then µA should get rotated, as well. (Of course, rotational invariance of the law of ω
would still be essential for the equality in law discussed in Remark 6.2.)
   However, the rotational invariance of the scaling limit is in fact used here, in a
somewhat implicit way, through the fact that the normalization factor F () in (4.39)
does not depend on θ, which was one of the implications of Proposition 4.9.
   We will see the same phenomenon in the proofs below: the conformal covariance
comes in some sense from the fact that the normalization factor cannot be changed
when applying a conformal map.

6.2    Scaling covariance
We show here the following special case of Theorem 6.1:
Proposition 6.4. Let A be some proper annulus of the plane and λ > 0 some scaling
factor. Then, for any B ⊂ ∆:

                               µλA (λB, λω) = λ3/4 µA (B, ω) .                           (6.2)

Proof. By (4.39), we have the L2 -limits

                                       Y λ,λA (λB, λω)       Y ,A (B, ω)
                  µλA (λB, λω) = lim                    = lim              ,
                                   →0       F (λ)       →0    F (λ)
where the second equality is just a tautology even for fixed  > 0. So, in order to
get the right side of (6.2), we need that lim→0 α4 (λ, 1)/α4 (, 1) = λ5/4 . By the scale
invariance of the scaling limit, α4 (λ, 1) = α4 (, 1/λ), so the ratio limit result (4.28)
finishes the proof.

A detail that might be worth pointing out is why it is that the covariance exponent

                                                         84
is given by the 4-arm exponent also close to ∂Q and not by the half-plane 3-arm
event (and the 2-arm event at the corners). The reason is that although the -boxes
counted in the macroscopic approximation Y  that are close to ∂Q indeed need to have
more-or-less the half-plane 3-arm event, but, on this macroscopic scale, we can use
conformal invariance combined with the effect of the normalization constant being still
the whole plane 4-arm probability. This is the same effect that was pointed out in
the last paragraph of Subsection 6.1 and was seen in Subsection 6.2. This works fine
because the normalization constant comes from the microscopic scale, and there, inside
the -box, again the whole-plane 4-arm event is the relevant.

A     Appendix: The strong separation phenomenon
In many planar statistical physics models, it is a very useful phenomenon that if one
conditions on certain curves (trajectories or interfaces) to reach to a long distance with-
out colliding with each other, then with a probability uniformly bounded away from
zero, they arrive at their target with a good separation, i.e., with a distance from each
other that is as large as it can be (up to a constant factor). Such a result was proba-
bly first proved and used in Kesten’s fundamental paper [Kes87]: conditioned on the
alternating four-arm event in A(r, R), with positive probability there are four inter-
faces well-separated at distance R. He used this to prove the quasi-multiplicativity
of multi-arms probabilities. Cleaner proofs appear in [SSt10, Appendix] and [Nol08].
However, this is weaker than what we need here: we want the conclusion under con-
ditioning on arbitrarily bad starting points of the four given interfaces at radius r.
Such a strong separation lemma was proved for Brownian motions by Greg Lawler in
[Law98, Lemma 4.2], which is a fundamental tool in computing Brownian intersection
exponents [LSW02]. Then, using the Lawler-strategy, an analogous result was proved
for a random walk approaching a level line of the discrete Gaussian free field in [SSh09,
Lemma 3.15], and for the meeting of a random walk and a loop-erased random walk in
[Mas09, Theorem 4.7], used again in [BM10]. This strategy could also be adapted to
percolation interfaces; however, as was kindly explained to us by Artëm Sapozhnikov,
it is simpler to modify Kesten’s argument. That approach has appeared in [DS11], but,
for completeness, roughly following their argument but in a form more suitable for us,
we include it here. The main ingredients of Kesten’s strategy are the same as those
of Lawler’s, just the organization of the ideas is different; e.g., the latter uses random
stopping times that the former does not. Consequently, in Kesten’s strategy it is easier
to separate the input that is needed from the model itself in order for the argument to
work. To emphasize its universal aspect, in the second part of this Appendix we will
use Kesten’s strategy to prove Lawler’s separation lemma for Brownian motions. We
hope that this mostly self-contained Appendix will be useful for other models, as well.


                                                       86
    The Lawler-strategy was streamlined and used in [LV12] to show strong separation
and coupling results for three-dimensional Brownian motions. This shows that the
separation phenomenon is not restricted to planar models, even if proving the separation
of interface surfaces in the three-dimensional critical percolation is presently just a
dream, especially that the RSW technology does not really exist yet.

A.1     Percolation interfaces
Let us stress that the results in this section hold for critical percolation on any planar
lattice where the RSW estimates are known; in particular, for bond percolation on Z2
and site percolation on T.
    Recall the notations from the beginning of Section 3. Our main goal is a proof of
Lemma 3.3, but we will first prove a more traditional version, where there is no “forward
conditioning” (i.e., the conditioned target for the interfaces is at the same radius where
we want the good separation), and there is no UΘ = τ conditioning.

Proposition A.1 (Strong Separation Lemma, [DS11]). Fix N ∈ 2Z+ for the number of
interfaces considered, and let A = A(R1 , R2 ) be the annulus centered around 0 with radii
100N η < 2R1 < R2 . Assume we are given some configuration of faces Θ = {θ1 , . . . , θN }
around the square of radius R2 , with some arbitrary initial quality Q(Θ).
    Let AΘ (R1 , R2 ) be the event that the N -tuple of interfaces in DΘ that start at the
N endpoints of Θ reach radius R1 , and let Γ be the set of these interfaces. Then, there
is some constant c(N ) > 0 such that
                           h      1                    i
                         P Q(Γ) >         AΘ (R1 , R2 ) > c(N ) .
                                  N
Proof. Let us start with a sketch of the main ideas. In the unconditional measure,
it is unlikely that in a fixed dyadic annulus A(s, 2s) there are interfaces very close to
each other; this is formalized in the well-known Lemma A.3 below, proved by RSW
estimates. Hence, still in the unconditional measure, the probability of fulfilling the
conditioning but having very low quality configurations on k consecutive dyadic scales
is exponentially small in k, with a base that can be made arbitrarily small if the “low
quality” is chosen low enough. On the other hand, from a dyadic scale with a not
very low quality, with some small probability the situation can be improved to a good
quality in the next dyadic scale, and this good quality then can be preserved along
several scales, with an exponentially small probability but with a uniformly positive
base (by the also standard (A.5) and (A.6) below). These suggest that conditioned on
AΘ (R1 , R2 ), if the starting quality at R2 was not very bad, then good quality scales
would appear with a positive frequency, and having a good quality at the end would
have positive probability. However, we start with an arbitrary starting configuration,
so we need to improve its quality little by little, with each step having a size comparable
to the quality at that moment.

                                            87
    Since the starting configuration might not be uniformly bad, the step sizes should
also vary locally. Therefore, we build a simple hierarchical structure on the interface
endpoints V = {x1 , . . . , xN } ⊂ B(R2 ) of the starting configuration: we first try to
improve the quality in small steps (in annuli on dyadic scales) for the interfaces that
are very close, then other interfaces join in at larger scales given by the distances in
the starting configuration, and so on, resulting in a tree structure. Here is the precise
procedure:
    Let the minimum distance between the points xi be s. For j ∈ N, let Gj be the graph
on V where two points are joined if their `∞ -distance is less than s2j ; in particular, G0
is the graph on V with no edges. If j ∈ N+ and C ⊆ V is a connected component of
Gj , but is not connected in Gj−1 , then C is called a level j cluster of V . The level of
a cluster is denoted by j(C). Note that if two clusters intersect, then one contains the
other. There is an obvious tree structure on the clusters, with V (as a single cluster)
being the root, and the singletons {xi } being the leaves. The parent of a cluster C will
be denoted by C p .
    For each cluster C ⊆ V , the edges between nearest neighbour points inside C can
be represented by the shorter arc in ∂B(R2 ) between them, and the union of these
arcs is a connected arc, denoted by [C] ⊆ ∂B(R2 ). For C = V , it can happen that
[C] = ∂B(R2 ). We now define a sequence of bounding boxes for each cluster C,

                    Bi (C) := x ∈ DΘ : dist∞ (x, [C]) ≤ s2j(C)−2+i ,
                                

for i = 0, 1, . . . , J(C) := j(C p ) − j(C) − 1. These boxes are not always rectangles, for
two reasons: the arcs [C] might contain corners of B(R2 ), and part of the boundary of
a box might come from Θ; see Figure A.1. We will call B0 (C) the inner bounding box
of C, and BJ (C) = BJ(C) (C) the outer bounding box of C. It may happen, of course,
that B0 (C) = BJ (C).
    Note that for disjoint clusters we always have BJ (C1 ) ∩ BJ (C2 ) = ∅. Moreover,
                                                   p    p           p           p
           dist∞ BJ (C1 ), BJ (C2 ) ≥ s(2max{j(C1 ),j(C2 )}−1 − 2j(C1 )−3 − 2j(C2 )−3 )
                                      
                                           p
                                   ≥ s2j(Ci )−2     for i = 1, 2.                     (A.1)

Similarly, if C1 $ C2 , then

                         dist∞ ∂BJ (C1 ), ∂BJ (C2 ) ≥ s2j(C2 )−3 .

Furthermore, it is clear that the `∞ -diameter of a bounding box satisfies

                        s2j(C)−1+i ≤ diam∞ (Bi (C)) ≤ N s2j(C)+i .                    (A.3)

These estimates mean that the boundaries of different bounding boxes are well-separated,
with distances at least on the order of the sizes of the boxes themselves.
   Let C be the collection of all the bounding boxes Bi (C) of all clusters with j(C) ≥ 1
and N s2j(C)+i ≤ R2 /4. The union of them is contained in B(R2 ) \ B(3R2 /4). In some

    We will use two lemmas, which are direct adaptations of widely used basic results
regarding separation of interfaces to our situation. For the first one, see, e.g., [SSt10,
Lemma A.3]; the second one comes from [SSt10, Lemma A.2] or [Kes87, Lemma 2].
Both are easily proved by RSW and FKG techniques. That the RSW technology works
nicely in our situation is ensured by the inequalities (A.1, A.2, A.3). Note that a
good quality implies that the interfaces can be continued nicely with RSW and FKG
gluing techniques, despite the fact that we require only that the endpoints have a
large distance, while a piece of a neighbouring interface γi±1 still can come close to an
endpoint yi . The reason that this works is that the neighbouring interface has the right
colour on its side closer to yi . See Figure A.2.

                                           92
    Let us conclude with a discussion of what even stronger versions one might imagine.
Two overly naive questions closely related to each other: (a) Could the lower bound
c(N ) on the success probability approach 1 as R2 /R1 tends to ∞? (b) Do the interfaces
become well-separated quickly, say, by radius R2 /2, and remain so all along till R1 ?
The answer to both, of course, is “no”, because there are many scales, and even from a
small quality at some scale we still have some chance to fulfill the conditioning. Another
direction is to ask how c(N ) depends on N . From the proof strategy it appears that a
larger N does not make it harder for neighboring interfaces to be about 1/N -separated.
However, a larger N also means more randomness, hence the typical quality at R1
should not be on the order of 1/N , only at most 1/(N logb N ), so c(N ) is not expected
to be independent of N . What seems likely is that if we look at the interface endpoints
at R1 locally, around some point of ∂B(R1 ), rescaled by N , then we get a translation-
invariant point process on R in the N → ∞ limit, which should have some repulsion
similar to the eigenvalue processes in random matrix theory. See [Dub07] for the closely
related question of growing SLEκ curves conditioned on not to intersect each other.
    Finally, there could be a “super-strong” version that we do not know how to prove,
though we expect it to be true:
Conjecture A.4 (Super-strong Separation Lemma). Given an arbitrary starting con-
figuration Θ of faces around B(R2 ) (with any number of faces), condition on at least
four of the interfaces starting from the endpoints of the faces to reach B(R1 ). Under
this conditioning, the set of interfaces reaching R1 have positive quality with positive
probability.
   If we condition on a Θ with N faces, then we can apply the Strong Separation
Lemma for 4 interfaces, and lose a factor of N4 in the probability. But for a general
Θ, the number of faces could be even on the order of R2 /η, so the loss would be huge.

A.2     Brownian intersections
We will now sketch a proof of the following basic result:
Proposition A.5 (Lawler’s Separation Lemma [Law98]). Let B(r) and B(R) be the
Euclidean disks around the origin, with 0 < 2r < R, and let Γ = {γ1 (t), γ2 (t)} be two
independent planar Brownian motions, started at arbitrary but different points γi (0) ∈
∂B(R), stopped when reaching ∂B(r), at stopping times τi (r). Then there is some
absolute constant c > 0 such that
                  h                                                i
                P Q(Γ(r)) > 1/4 γ1 [0, τ1 (r)] ∩ γ2 [0, τ2 (r)] = ∅ > c ,

where Γ(s) is the pair of Brownian motions, each stopped at τi (s), r ≤ s ≤ R, and
Q(Γ(s)) is the quality at ∂B(s), defined by
                              1                                    
                  Q(Γ(s)) = min dist γi (τi (s)), γ3−i [0, τ3−i (s)] .
                              s i=1,2

                                           93
    Lemma 4.2 in [Law98] is more general than this, involving packets of Brownian
motions, but the ideas are exactly the same, so we chose the notationally simplest
possible setting. Also, the Brownian motions could be started outside B(R), and we
could condition on their trajectories up to their first hitting of ∂B(R); the proof would
be exactly the same.
    As opposed to percolation interfaces, where the closeness of one side of a neighbour-
ing interface does not present any danger to fulfilling the conditioning, see Figure A.2,
a Brownian motion could hit another trajectory anywhere, causing failure. That is why
the notion of quality is strengthened as above.
Proof. The following two lemmas are the analogs of Lemmas A.2 and A.3. For sim-
plicity, we state them for ordinary qualities instead of the relative ones introduced
in (A.4).
Lemma A.6. For any ρ > 0 there is an (ρ) > 0 with
                      h           1i                    
                    P Q(Γ(s/2)) >    > (ρ) P Q(Γ(s)) > ρ ,
                                  4
whenever r ≤ s/2 < s ≤ R.
Proof. Given any pair Γ(s) satisfying Q(Γ(s)) > ρ, it is straightforward to construct
two disjoint domains in the plane, U1 and U2 , with the following properties, as depicted
on the left part of Figure A.3: the interior of each Ui is disjoint from γ3−i [0, τ3−i (s)]
and from B(s/2), but contains the sρ/2-ball around γi (τi (s)); ∂Ui contains an arc of
∂B(s/2), called Vi ; the harmonic measure of Vi for Brownian motion in Ui started from
γi (τi (s)) is at least h(ρ) > 0, independently of s; and finally, V1 and V2 are well-separated
in the sense that if each γi exits Ui at Vi , then we necessarily have Q(Γ(s/2)) > 1/4.
This proves the lemma with (ρ) = h(ρ)2 .

Lemma A.7. For any δ > 0, if ρ = ρ(δ) > 0 is small enough, then, for arbitrary but
different starting points γi (0) ∈ ∂B(s),
                 h                                                      i
                P γ1 [0, τ1 (s/2)] ∩ γ2 [0, τ2 (s/2)] = ∅, Q(Γ(s/2)) ≤ ρ < δ .
Proof. Let γ ∗ be the subpath of γ1 [0, τ1 (s/2)] from the last time it entered the ball of
radius s/4 around z := γ1 (τ1 (s/2)) till its end τ1 (s/2). If the event {Q(Γ(s/2)) ≤ ρ}
                                                                      √
occurs, then there is a first time that γ2 enters the ball of radius s ρ around z; let us
denote the entering point by y. The connected component of Bz (s/4)\(B(s/2)∪γ ∗ ) that
contains y will be denoted by D, and the part of ∂B(s/2)∩∂D that has distance between
sρ and s/4 from z will be denoted by β. See the right hand picture of Figure A.3. It is
now an easy exercise about harmonic measure to show that, regardless of what γ ∗ and
y are, the probability that a Brownian motion started at y exits D not through γ ∗ ∪ β
is close to zero if ρ is small, which implies the lemma.
   Based on these two lemmas, the rest of the proof of Proposition A.5 is identical to
that of Proposition A.1.
